games.title: Daniell cell checks
items: With 1 mol dm⁻³ solutions, a Daniell cell gives about 1.1 V.
When the opposing external voltage equals 1.1 V, no current flows.
In a galvanic cell, electrical energy is used to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.
The salt bridge allows electrons to flow between the two solutions.
Ions, not electrons, move through the salt bridge; electrons travel in the external wire.
Above 1.1 V of opposing voltage, zinc gets deposited at the zinc electrode.
The reaction is reversed, so Zn²⁺ is reduced to Zn.

quiz.q: What is the overall reaction in a Daniell cell?
quiz.explain: Zinc, the stronger reducing agent, is oxidised and Cu²⁺ is reduced to copper.
steps: In a Daniell cell zinc is oxidised: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻.
Cu²⁺ is reduced: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; adding the halves gives the overall reaction.
Answer: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
quiz.mistake: Writes the reverse, non-spontaneous reaction

quiz.q: A Daniell cell is opposed by an external voltage of 0.8 V. In which direction do electrons flow in the outer circuit?
options: From the copper rod to the zinc rod
From the zinc rod to the copper rod
Electrons flow through the salt bridge
quiz.explain: 0.8 V is less than 1.1 V, so the cell still works normally: electrons leave zinc and go to copper.
steps: Opposing voltage 0.8 V is less than the cell's 1.1 V.
So the cell still works normally: electrons flow from zinc to copper.
Answer: From the zinc rod to the copper rod
quiz.mistake: Thinks any opposing voltage reverses the cell

quiz.q: What is the main function of a salt bridge?
options: It supplies Cu²⁺ ions to the cathode
It carries electrons between the electrodes
It completes the circuit and maintains electrical neutrality of the two solutions
quiz.explain: Ions migrate through the bridge to balance charges building up in the half-cells, keeping the current flowing.
steps: Ions migrate through the salt bridge to balance charge in each half-cell.
This completes the inner circuit and keeps both solutions neutral; electrons never pass through it.
Answer: It completes the circuit and maintains electrical neutrality of the two solutions
quiz.mistake: Thinks electrons pass through the solution

quiz.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a galvanic cell from an electrolytic cell?
options: Both convert electrical energy into chemical energy
A galvanic cell needs an external battery
An electrolytic cell is driven by a spontaneous reaction
A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy; an electrolytic cell does the reverse
quiz.explain: Galvanic cells run on spontaneous reactions; electrolytic cells need external electricity to drive non-spontaneous ones.
steps: A galvanic cell uses a spontaneous reaction to give electrical energy.
An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.
Answer: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy; an electrolytic cell does the reverse
quiz.mistake: Swaps the energy conversions

quiz.q: When the opposing external voltage on a Daniell cell is raised above 1.1 V, which process takes place at the copper electrode?
quiz.explain: The reaction reverses: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the copper electrode while Zn²⁺ is reduced at the zinc electrode.
steps: Above 1.1 V the cell reaction is reversed.
At the copper electrode Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, so copper dissolves.
Answer: Copper dissolves as Cu²⁺
quiz.mistake: Assumes the electrode reactions stay the same

quiz.q: Which industrial process is an application of electrolytic cells?
options: Production of sodium hydroxide and chlorine from brine
Burning coal in a thermal plant
quiz.explain: The chlor-alkali process electrolyses brine to give NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂.
steps: Electrolytic cells use electricity to make chemicals.
Electrolysis of brine gives NaOH and Cl₂ (chlor-alkali process).
Answer: Production of sodium hydroxide and chlorine from brine
quiz.mistake: Confuses electrolysis with ordinary thermal reactions

quiz.q: At what external opposing voltage does a standard Daniell cell stop delivering current?
quiz.explain: Current stops when the external voltage exactly equals the cell potential of 1.1 V.
steps: Current stops when the opposing voltage exactly balances the cell potential.
The standard Daniell cell potential is 1.1 V.
Answer: 1.1 V
quiz.mistake: Uses one electrode potential instead of the cell potential

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A Daniell cell can be made to work as an electrolytic cell. Reason (R): Applying an external voltage greater than 1.1 V in opposition reverses the cell reaction.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Above 1.1 V the reaction is driven backwards using external electricity, which is exactly what an electrolytic cell does.
steps: A: a Daniell cell can work as an electrolytic cell. True.
R: an opposing voltage above 1.1 V reverses the reaction. True.
Driving the reverse reaction with external electricity is electrolysis, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see that reversing the reaction makes it electrolytic

teach.ask: Gappu holds a battery: 'What is the difference between a galvanic cell and an electrolytic cell?'
teach.praise: Zap! Galvanic cells turn a spontaneous reaction into electricity; electrolytic cells use electricity to force a reaction. Got it!
teach.nudge: Which one makes electricity from a spontaneous reaction, and what does the other one need?

revise.summary: A galvanic cell turns a spontaneous redox reaction into electricity; an electrolytic cell uses electricity for a non-spontaneous one. The Daniell cell, Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, gives 1.1 V; an opposing voltage above 1.1 V reverses it. A salt bridge completes the circuit and keeps solutions neutral.
remember: Daniell cell: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), 1.1 V
External voltage < 1.1 V: normal; = 1.1 V: no current; > 1.1 V: reversed
Salt bridge: KCl or KNO₃ in agar
traps: Don't say electrons flow through the salt bridge
Don't reverse the Daniell reaction: zinc is oxidised

topics.title: Galvanic cells: half-cells, notation and the SHE

learn.hook: Cell notation is chemistry's shorthand. Zn|Zn²⁺||Cu²⁺|Cu tells an examiner the whole story in one line, if you know how to read it.
points: A galvanic cell has two half-cells (redox couples). Oxidation occurs at the anode, which is negative in a galvanic cell; reduction occurs at the cathode, which is positive.
Notation: anode on the left, cathode on the right, a single vertical line for a phase boundary and a double line for the salt bridge: Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(aq)||Cu²⁺(aq)|Cu(s).
E_cell = E_right − E_left = E_cathode − E_anode, using reduction potentials for both.
Single electrode potentials cannot be measured alone. The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), Pt(s)|H₂(g, 1 bar)|H⁺(aq, 1 M), is assigned 0.00 V at all temperatures.
Measured against SHE: Pt|H₂(1 bar)|H⁺(1 M)||Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu gives 0.34 V, so E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V; the zinc cell gives E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V.

example.q: Write the cell for the reaction 2Ag⁺(aq) + Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s) and find E°cell. E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V.
steps: Zn is oxidised, so it is the anode (left); Ag⁺ is reduced at the cathode (right)
Cell: Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(aq)||Ag⁺(aq)|Ag(s)
E°cell = E°right − E°left = 0.80 − (−0.76)

learn.reallife: Chemistry labs at IISERs calibrate reference electrodes against the hydrogen electrode, the zero point on which every textbook E° value is built.

games.title: Read the cell notation left to right

quiz.q: What is E°cell for Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(aq)||Ag⁺(aq)|Ag(s)? E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V (in V).
quiz.explain: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. Doubling for 2Ag⁺ does not change E°.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order or doubles the silver potential
steps: E°cell = E°right − E°left
Answer: 1.56

quiz.q: In a galvanic cell, where does oxidation take place and what is its polarity?
options: At the cathode, which is positive
At the anode, which is positive
At the cathode, which is negative
At the anode, which is negative
quiz.explain: Oxidation releases electrons at the anode, making it the negative terminal of a galvanic cell.
steps: Oxidation releases electrons at the anode.
Electrons pile up there, so in a galvanic cell the anode is negative.
Answer: At the anode, which is negative
quiz.mistake: Uses the electrolytic-cell polarity for a galvanic cell

quiz.q: What potential is assigned to the standard hydrogen electrode?
quiz.explain: By convention, E°(H⁺/½H₂) = 0 at all temperatures; other potentials are measured against it.
steps: By convention, the SHE is assigned 0.00 V at all temperatures.
Other electrode potentials are measured against it.
Answer: 0.00 V at all temperatures
quiz.mistake: Thinks the SHE value is measured, not assigned

quiz.q: A cell is written Pt(s)|H₂(g, 1 bar)|H⁺(aq, 1 M)||Cu²⁺(aq, 1 M)|Cu(s) and its emf is 0.34 V. What does this tell us?
options: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, and Cu²⁺ is reduced more easily than H⁺
Hydrogen ions are reduced at copper
quiz.explain: With SHE on the left as anode, E°cell = E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) − 0 = +0.34 V, so copper is the cathode.
steps: SHE is on the left (anode, 0.00 V), so E°cell = E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) − 0.
E°cell = +0.34 V, so E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and Cu²⁺ is reduced (copper is the cathode).
Answer: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, and Cu²⁺ is reduced more easily than H⁺
quiz.mistake: Puts the electrode on the right as the anode

quiz.q: Which is the correct representation of the cell with the reaction Mg(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s)?
quiz.explain: The anode (Mg, oxidised) is written on the left, the cathode (Ag⁺/Ag) on the right, with || for the salt bridge.
steps: Mg is oxidised, so it is the anode, written on the left: Mg(s)|Mg²⁺(aq).
Ag⁺ is reduced at the cathode, on the right: Ag⁺(aq)|Ag(s), with || for the salt bridge.
Answer: Mg(s)|Mg²⁺(aq)||Ag⁺(aq)|Ag(s)
quiz.mistake: Puts the cathode on the left

quiz.q: A cell made of Zn²⁺/Zn (E° = −0.76 V) and SHE: which electrode is the cathode?
quiz.explain: Zinc has the lower reduction potential, so it is oxidised (anode); H⁺ is reduced at the SHE (cathode).
steps: E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V is lower than SHE's 0.00 V.
So zinc is oxidised (anode) and H⁺ is reduced at the SHE (cathode).
Answer: The standard hydrogen electrode
quiz.mistake: Assumes the metal electrode is always the cathode

quiz.q: Why can the absolute potential of a single electrode not be measured?
options: Only a potential difference between two electrodes can be measured
quiz.explain: A voltmeter needs two terminals, so potentials are measured relative to a reference like SHE.
steps: A voltmeter measures only a difference between two terminals.
So a single electrode potential can only be found against a reference like SHE.
Answer: Only a potential difference between two electrodes can be measured
quiz.mistake: Thinks a single electrode can be connected alone

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In a galvanic cell the cathode is the positive electrode. Reason (R): Electrons are consumed at the cathode by the reduction half-reaction.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Electrons flow towards the cathode where they are used up in reduction, making it positive relative to the anode.
steps: A: the cathode is positive in a galvanic cell. True.
R: electrons are consumed at the cathode in reduction. True.
Using up electrons makes it positive relative to the anode, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Uses the electrolytic-cell sign convention

teach.ask: Gappu stares at Zn|Zn²⁺||Cu²⁺|Cu: 'What do all these lines mean, and how do I get the cell voltage?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Anode on the left, cathode on the right, salt bridge in the middle, and E_cell = E_right − E_left!
teach.nudge: Which electrode goes on the left, and how do you combine the two reduction potentials?

revise.summary: A galvanic cell has oxidation at the negative anode and reduction at the positive cathode; notation puts the anode left and cathode right with || for the salt bridge. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. The SHE is 0.00 V; E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V.
focus: Anode and cathode: process and sign
traps: Don't call the galvanic anode positive
Don't subtract the cathode from the anode

topics.title: Electrochemical series and predicting reactions

learn.hook: Can you store copper sulphate solution in a zinc pot from the market? The electrochemical series answers in one glance.
points: Standard reduction potentials (1 M, 1 bar, 298 K) listed in order form the electrochemical series: F₂/F⁻ +2.87 V at the top, Li⁺/Li −3.05 V at the bottom.

The higher (more positive) E°, the stronger the oxidised form as an oxidising agent: F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent. The lower (more negative) E°, the stronger the reduced form as a reducing agent: Li is the strongest reducing agent.
A redox reaction is feasible if E°cell = E°(species reduced) − E°(species oxidised) is positive. A metal with negative E° can liberate H₂ from dilute acids; Cu (+0.34 V) cannot.
Inert electrodes such as platinum or gold carry electrons for couples with no solid metal, e.g. Pt(s)|Fe³⁺, Fe²⁺ or Pt(s)|H₂|H⁺.
Useful values: Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44, H⁺/H₂ 0.00, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34, I₂/I⁻ +0.54, Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77, Ag⁺/Ag +0.80, Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V.

example.q: Can CuSO₄ solution be stored in a zinc vessel? E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V.
steps: Possible reaction: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu
Positive E°cell means the reaction occurs, so zinc would dissolve
example.answer: No — zinc reduces Cu²⁺ and the vessel would be eaten away

learn.reallife: Galvanised iron buckets and water tanks sold in Indian markets rely on zinc's lower E°: zinc corrodes first and protects the iron underneath.

games.title: Arrange by standard reduction potential
games.prompt: Most negative E° to most positive E°

games.title: Feasible or not?
items: Zinc liberates H₂ from dilute HCl.
E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) is negative, so E°cell with H⁺/H₂ is positive.
Copper liberates H₂ from dilute HCl.
E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) is +0.34 V, so the reaction has negative E°cell.
Fe³⁺ can oxidise I⁻ to I₂.
Silver nitrate solution can be safely stored in a copper vessel.
Cu (0.34 V) reduces Ag⁺ (0.80 V), so copper dissolves.
Li is the strongest reducing agent in the series.
It has the most negative reduction potential, −3.05 V.
F⁻ is a strong reducing agent.
F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent, so F⁻ is an extremely weak reducing agent.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest oxidising agent among these? E°: Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V, Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V.
quiz.explain: The species with the highest reduction potential is most easily reduced, i.e. it is the strongest oxidising agent.
steps: The strongest oxidising agent is the species most easily reduced: highest E°.
Highest E° here is Cl₂/Cl⁻ at +1.36 V.
Answer: Cl₂
quiz.mistake: Chooses the metal with the lowest E°

quiz.q: Which metal is the strongest reducing agent? E°: Mg²⁺/Mg −2.36 V, Al³⁺/Al −1.66 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V.
quiz.explain: The most negative E° means the metal is most easily oxidised, so it is the best reducing agent.
steps: The strongest reducing agent is most easily oxidised: most negative E°.
Most negative here is Mg²⁺/Mg at −2.36 V.
Answer: Mg
quiz.mistake: Picks the least negative value

quiz.q: Can a solution of CuSO₄ be stored in a silver vessel? E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V.
options: Yes, because CuSO₄ reacts with silver to protect it
Yes, because Ag cannot reduce Cu²⁺
quiz.explain: For Ag + Cu²⁺ → Ag⁺ + Cu, E°cell = 0.34 − 0.80 = −0.46 V, so no reaction occurs.
steps: Check Ag + Cu²⁺ → Ag⁺ + Cu: E°cell = E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) − E°(Ag⁺/Ag).
E°cell = 0.34 − 0.80 = −0.46 V, negative, so no reaction: Ag cannot reduce Cu²⁺.
Answer: Yes, because Ag cannot reduce Cu²⁺
quiz.mistake: Assumes every metal reacts with every salt solution

quiz.q: Will Fe³⁺ oxidise I⁻ to I₂ under standard conditions? E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V, E°(I₂/I⁻) = +0.54 V. What is E°cell (in V)?
quiz.explain: E°cell = 0.77 − 0.54 = +0.23 V; positive, so the reaction is feasible.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order and gets a negative value
steps: Reduced species: Fe³⁺ (0.77 V); oxidised: I⁻ (0.54 V)
Answer: 0.23

quiz.q: Why does copper not liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: Its standard reduction potential is negative
Its standard reduction potential is positive, higher than that of H⁺/H₂
HCl is too weak an acid
quiz.explain: With E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, the reaction Cu + 2H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + H₂ has E°cell = −0.34 V.
steps: For Cu + 2H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + H₂: E°cell = 0.00 − 0.34 = −0.34 V.
Negative E°cell, so copper cannot liberate H₂; its E° is positive, above H⁺/H₂.
Answer: Its standard reduction potential is positive, higher than that of H⁺/H₂
quiz.mistake: Thinks all metals react with acids

quiz.q: Why is platinum used as the electrode in the Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ half-cell?
options: It is inert and only provides a surface for electron transfer
quiz.explain: There is no solid metal in this couple, so an inert conductor like Pt is needed to carry electrons without reacting.
steps: The Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ couple has no solid metal.
Platinum is inert and only provides a surface for electron transfer.
Answer: It is inert and only provides a surface for electron transfer
quiz.mistake: Thinks the electrode metal must take part in the reaction

quiz.q: Arrange the metals in increasing order of reducing power: Ag (+0.80 V), Zn (−0.76 V), Cu (+0.34 V), Mg (−2.36 V).
quiz.explain: Reducing power increases as E° becomes more negative.
steps: Reducing power increases as E° becomes more negative.
So increasing reducing power: Ag < Cu < Zn < Mg.
Answer: Ag < Cu < Zn < Mg
quiz.mistake: Ranks by the size of the number without considering the sign

quiz.q: Assertion (A): F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent. Reason (R): F₂/F⁻ has the highest standard reduction potential in the electrochemical series.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: The highest E° means F₂ has the greatest tendency to be reduced, so it oxidises others most strongly.
steps: A: F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent. True.
R: F₂/F⁻ has the highest standard reduction potential. True.
Highest E° means greatest tendency to be reduced, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link high reduction potential to oxidising strength

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I use the electrochemical series to tell if a metal will push hydrogen out of an acid?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Metals with negative E° sit below hydrogen and give positive E°cell with acid, so they release H₂!
teach.nudge: You mentioned the table, but what sign of E° does a metal need, and what must E°cell be?

revise.summary: Standard reduction potentials in order form the electrochemical series, from F₂/F⁻ (+2.87 V) to Li⁺/Li (−3.05 V). Higher E° means a stronger oxidising agent; lower E° a stronger reducing agent. A reaction is feasible if E°cell is positive; metals with negative E° liberate H₂ from dilute acids.
focus: Reading oxidising and reducing strength from E°
remember: Strongest oxidising agent: F₂; strongest reducing agent: Li
traps: Don't say a more negative E° means a stronger oxidising agent
Don't forget copper cannot displace H₂ from dilute acids

topics.title: The Nernst equation

learn.hook: Standard conditions are rare outside the textbook. Walther Nernst's equation tells you the real voltage when concentrations are anything but 1 M.
points: For a reduction Mⁿ⁺(aq) + ne⁻ → M(s): E = E° − (RT/nF) ln(1/[Mⁿ⁺]). At 298 K this becomes E = E° − (0.059/n) log(1/[Mⁿ⁺]).
For a whole cell aA + bB → cC + dD: E_cell = E°cell − (0.059/n) log Q at 298 K, where Q = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ ÷ [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ (pure solids and liquids are left out).
For the Daniell cell: E_cell = 1.10 − (0.059/2) log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]). Raising [Cu²⁺] or lowering [Zn²⁺] increases E_cell.
Hydrogen electrode at 1 bar: E = −0.059 pH at 298 K.

example.q: Find E_cell at 298 K for Zn|Zn²⁺(0.01 M)||Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu. E°cell = 1.10 V.
steps: log Q = −2

learn.reallife: The pH meters used in Indian dairies and water-testing labs are electrochemical cells: their reading changes by 0.059 V for every pH unit, straight from the Nernst equation.

items.text: At 298 K, E_cell = E°cell − (___/n) log Q.
For Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, n = ___.
Pure solids such as Zn(s) are ___ from the reaction quotient Q.
For a hydrogen electrode at 1 bar and 298 K, E = −0.059 × ___.

quiz.q: Calculate E_cell at 298 K for Zn|Zn²⁺(0.01 M)||Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu, given E°cell = 1.10 V (answer in V).
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign error with log Q, giving 1.041 V
steps: Answer: 1.159

quiz.q: What is the electrode potential (in V) of Cu²⁺(0.01 M)/Cu at 298 K? E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V.
quiz.mistake: Adds the correction instead of subtracting
steps: Answer: 0.281

quiz.q: What is the potential (in V) of a hydrogen electrode in a solution of pH 3 at 298 K (H₂ at 1 bar)?
quiz.mistake: Drops the negative sign
steps: Answer: -0.177

quiz.q: In the Daniell cell, how can E_cell be increased above 1.10 V?
options: Increase the length of the salt bridge
quiz.explain: E_cell = 1.10 − (0.059/2) log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]); a smaller ratio makes log Q negative and E_cell larger.
steps: A smaller ratio [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] makes log Q negative, raising E_cell.
So increase [Cu²⁺] or decrease [Zn²⁺].
Answer: Increase [Cu²⁺] or decrease [Zn²⁺]
quiz.mistake: Gets the reaction quotient upside down

quiz.q: For Mg(s)|Mg²⁺(0.001 M)||Cu²⁺(0.1 M)|Cu(s), E°cell = 2.70 V. What is E_cell at 298 K (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Inverts Q (uses [Cu²⁺]/[Mg²⁺]), giving 2.641 V
steps: Q = [Mg²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 10⁻²
Answer: 2.759

quiz.q: Why are concentrations of Zn(s) and Cu(s) not written in the Nernst equation for the Daniell cell?
options: They cancel out with the salt bridge
They are too small to measure
Solids do not take part in the reaction
Pure solids have constant activity taken as 1
quiz.explain: The activity of a pure solid is unity, so it does not appear in Q.
steps: The activity of a pure solid is constant and taken as 1.
So Zn(s) and Cu(s) do not appear in Q.
Answer: Pure solids have constant activity taken as 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks solids are not reactants or products

quiz.q: For Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s), E° = 0.80 V. What is E (in V) at 298 K when [Ag⁺] = 0.1 M?
quiz.mistake: Divides 0.059 by 2 although n = 1
steps: Answer: 0.741

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The emf of a cell changes when the concentrations of ions are changed. Reason (R): E°cell depends on the concentrations of the ions.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: E_cell changes with concentration through the log Q term, but E° is fixed (defined at 1 M), so R is false.
steps: A: emf changes when ion concentrations change. True, through the log Q term.
R: E°cell depends on concentrations. False: E° is fixed at standard 1 M conditions.
So A is true, R is false.
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Confuses E with E°

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Why isn't my cell giving exactly E°? What equation do I use for real concentrations?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The Nernst equation, E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q, corrects for concentrations. Real-world ready!
teach.nudge: Which equation, and what term in it carries the concentrations?

revise.summary: The Nernst equation gives electrode or cell potential at any concentration: E_cell = E°cell − (0.059/n) log Q at 298 K, leaving out pure solids and liquids. For the Daniell cell, raising [Cu²⁺] or lowering [Zn²⁺] increases E_cell. For a hydrogen electrode E = −0.059 pH.
focus: Writing the Nernst equation for an electrode and a cell
E of hydrogen electrode from pH
traps: Don't include solids in Q
Don't say E° changes with concentration
Don't forget to divide 0.059 by n

topics.title: Cell potential, Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant

learn.hook: A positive cell voltage is chemistry's green signal: it tells you the reaction is spontaneous and how far it will go before it stops.
points: Electrical work done by a cell = nFE_cell, so Δr G = −nFE_cell and Δr G° = −nFE°cell. F (Faraday constant) = 96487 C mol⁻¹, often taken as 96500 C mol⁻¹.
A positive E_cell gives a negative Δr G: the reaction is spontaneous.
At equilibrium E_cell = 0 and Q = K, so E°cell = (2.303RT/nF) log K_c = (0.059/n) log K_c at 298 K.
Also Δr G° = −2.303RT log K_c. A large positive E° means a very large K: the reaction goes nearly to completion.

example.q: Find Δr G° for the Daniell cell (E°cell = 1.10 V). Take F = 96500 C mol⁻¹.

learn.reallife: Electrochemists at CSIR-CECRI, Karaikudi, use exactly these relations to screen new battery chemistries: a bigger E° means more energy stored per mole.

games.title: From E° to K at 298 K
items: Write the balanced cell reaction and find n
Take the antilog to find K

quiz.q: What is Δr G° (in kJ mol⁻¹) for the Daniell cell with E°cell = 1.10 V? Take F = 96500 C mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Uses n = 1 or drops the negative sign
steps: Δr G° = −nFE°
= −212.3 kJ mol⁻¹
Answer: -212.3

quiz.q: A cell reaction with n = 2 has E°cell = 0.295 V at 298 K. What is log K_c?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by n
steps: log K = nE° ÷ 0.059
Answer: 10

quiz.q: What is the sign of Δr G for a reaction whose E_cell is positive?
options: Zero: the reaction is at equilibrium
quiz.explain: Δr G = −nFE_cell, so a positive E_cell gives a negative Δr G.
steps: Δr G = −nFE_cell.
A positive E_cell gives a negative Δr G, so the reaction is spontaneous.
Answer: Negative: the reaction is spontaneous
quiz.mistake: Assumes Δr G and E_cell have the same sign

quiz.q: What is E_cell for a galvanic cell whose reaction has reached equilibrium?
quiz.explain: At equilibrium Δr G = 0, so E_cell = 0; the battery is 'dead'.
steps: At equilibrium Δr G = 0.
Since Δr G = −nFE_cell, E_cell must be zero.
Answer: Zero
quiz.mistake: Thinks the cell potential becomes E° at equilibrium

quiz.q: For a reaction with n = 1 and E°cell = 0.118 V at 298 K, what is K_c?
quiz.mistake: Stops at log K = 2 and reports it as K
steps: Answer: 100

quiz.q: Calculate Δr G° (in kJ mol⁻¹) for a cell with n = 1 and E°cell = 0.46 V. Take F = 96500 C mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert J to kJ, or drops the sign
steps: Δr G° = −nFE°
= −44.39 kJ mol⁻¹
Answer: -44.39

quiz.q: A cell reaction has a very large positive E°cell. What can you say about its equilibrium constant?
options: It is very large; the reaction goes nearly to completion
It cannot be predicted from E°
quiz.explain: log K = nE°/0.059, so a large positive E° gives a very large K.
steps: log K = nE°/0.059 at 298 K.
A large positive E° gives a very large log K, so K is very large and the reaction goes nearly to completion.
Answer: It is very large; the reaction goes nearly to completion
quiz.mistake: Does not connect E° to K

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Electrical work done by a galvanic cell equals the decrease in its Gibbs energy. Reason (R): Δr G = −nFE_cell.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: The maximum electrical work obtainable is nFE_cell, which equals −Δr G; R states this relation.
steps: A: electrical work equals the decrease in Gibbs energy. True.
R: Δr G = −nFE_cell. True.
nFE_cell is the work, and it equals −Δr G, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see Δr G = −nFE as the work relation

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If a cell has a positive voltage, how do I know the reaction is spontaneous?'
teach.praise: Chirp! ΔG = −nFE, so positive E gives negative ΔG: spontaneous. Simple and powerful!
teach.nudge: Which thermodynamic quantity links to E_cell, and what sign does it take?

revise.summary: The electrical work of a cell is nFE_cell, so Δr G = −nFE_cell and Δr G° = −nFE°cell (F ≈ 96500 C mol⁻¹). Positive E_cell means spontaneous. At equilibrium E_cell = 0, and E°cell = (0.059/n) log K_c at 298 K; Δr G° = −2.303RT log K_c.
focus: Spontaneity from the sign of E_cell
traps: Don't forget the minus sign in Δr G = −nFE
Don't leave Δr G in J when kJ is asked (divide by 1000)

topics.title: Conductance, conductivity and molar conductivity

learn.hook: Tap water conducts electricity but distilled water barely does. Measuring that difference precisely is how labs check water purity.
points: Resistance R = ρ(l/A), where ρ is resistivity (Ω m). Conductance G = 1/R (siemens, S). Conductivity κ = 1/ρ (S m⁻¹, often S cm⁻¹; 1 S m⁻¹ = 0.01 S cm⁻¹).

Electronic (metallic) conduction depends on the metal's nature and structure and the number of valence electrons; it decreases as temperature rises. Electrolytic (ionic) conduction depends on the nature of the electrolyte, ion size and solvation, solvent viscosity, concentration and temperature; it increases as temperature rises.

Conductivity is measured in a conductivity cell (two Pt electrodes coated with Pt black) using a Wheatstone bridge with AC current, to avoid electrolysis and polarisation. Cell constant G* = l/A = R × κ.
Molar conductivity Λm = κ/c. In S cm² mol⁻¹: Λm = (κ in S cm⁻¹ × 1000) ÷ (molarity in mol L⁻¹). In SI it is S m² mol⁻¹.

example.q: A conductivity cell filled with 0.1 M KCl (κ = 0.0129 S cm⁻¹) has a resistance of 100 Ω. Find the cell constant and Λm.
steps: = 129 S cm² mol⁻¹
example.answer: G* = 1.29 cm⁻¹; Λm = 129 S cm² mol⁻¹

learn.reallife: Pharma companies in Baddi and Hyderabad monitor the conductivity of 'purified water' continuously; a rise warns that ions have crept in.

quiz.q: A conductivity cell with 0.1 M KCl (κ = 0.0129 S cm⁻¹) has resistance 100 Ω. What is the cell constant (in cm⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Divides κ by R instead of multiplying
steps: G* = κR
Answer: 1.29

quiz.q: What is Λm (in S cm² mol⁻¹) of 0.1 M KCl with κ = 0.0129 S cm⁻¹?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 1000 that converts litres to cm³
steps: Λm = 1000κ ÷ c
Answer: 129

quiz.q: The same cell (G* = 1.29 cm⁻¹) filled with a 0.02 M electrolyte shows R = 520 Ω. Its conductivity is n × 10⁻³ S cm⁻¹. What is n (two decimals)?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies G* by R instead of dividing (gives 670.8), or slips a power of ten
steps: κ = G* ÷ R
Answer: 2.48

quiz.q: Why is alternating current (AC) used to measure the resistance of an electrolytic solution?
options: To prevent electrolysis and polarisation at the electrodes
Because AC heats the solution evenly
Because DC cannot pass through solutions
quiz.explain: DC would decompose the electrolyte and change its composition at the electrodes; AC avoids this.
steps: DC would decompose the electrolyte at the electrodes and polarise them.
AC avoids electrolysis and polarisation, so the resistance measured is true.
Answer: To prevent electrolysis and polarisation at the electrodes
quiz.mistake: Thinks AC is chosen only for safety or heating

quiz.q: How does the conductivity of a metal and of an electrolyte change on heating?
quiz.explain: Heating increases vibrations of metal ions, hindering electrons; in solutions it lowers viscosity and speeds up ions.
steps: Metals: heating increases vibrations of metal ions, hindering electrons, so conductivity decreases.
Electrolytes: heating lowers viscosity and speeds ions, so conductivity increases.
Answer: Metal's decreases, electrolyte's increases
quiz.mistake: Assumes all conductors behave alike with temperature

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of molar conductivity?
quiz.explain: Λm = κ/c = (S m⁻¹) ÷ (mol m⁻³) = S m² mol⁻¹.
steps: Λm = κ ÷ c.
Units: (S m⁻¹) ÷ (mol m⁻³) = S m² mol⁻¹.
Answer: S m² mol⁻¹
quiz.mistake: Confuses molar conductivity with conductivity

quiz.q: A solution has resistivity 50 Ω cm. What is its conductivity (in S cm⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Treats conductivity as equal to resistivity
steps: κ = 1/ρ
Answer: 0.02

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The cell constant of a conductivity cell is found using a KCl solution of known conductivity. Reason (R): G* = κ × R, so knowing κ and measuring R gives G*.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Because l and A are hard to measure directly, a standard KCl solution is used with G* = κR.
steps: A: the cell constant is found using KCl of known conductivity. True.
R: G* = κ × R, so known κ and measured R give G*. True.
R explains how the KCl method works.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the calibration to the formula

teach.ask: Gappu dips a probe: 'What's the difference between conductance, conductivity and molar conductivity?'
teach.praise: Bzzt! Conductance is 1/R, conductivity is 1/ρ, and molar conductivity is κ divided by concentration. Electrifying!
teach.nudge: You defined one of them. How is molar conductivity obtained from conductivity?

revise.summary: Resistance R = ρ(l/A); conductance G = 1/R and conductivity κ = 1/ρ. Metallic conduction falls with temperature; ionic conduction rises. Conductivity is measured with AC in a conductivity cell, using cell constant G* = l/A = Rκ. Molar conductivity Λm = κ/c (κ × 1000 ÷ M in S cm² mol⁻¹).
focus: Definitions and units of R, G, κ, Λm
Measuring conductivity and the cell constant
remember: Λm (S cm² mol⁻¹) = κ (S cm⁻¹) × 1000 ÷ M
SI unit of Λm: S m² mol⁻¹
traps: Don't forget the factor 1000 when using S cm⁻¹ and mol L⁻¹
Don't say metallic conductivity rises with temperature

topics.title: Variation with concentration and Kohlrausch's law

learn.hook: Dilute a salt solution and its conductivity falls, yet its molar conductivity rises. It sounds like a contradiction until you count ions properly.
points: Conductivity κ decreases on dilution because the number of ions per unit volume falls. Molar conductivity Λm increases on dilution because Λm = κV, and V (volume containing 1 mol) increases more than κ falls.
Limiting molar conductivity Λ°m is the value as concentration approaches zero.

Strong electrolytes: Λm = Λ°m − A c^½ (Debye–Hückel–Onsager). Λm rises slowly on dilution; a plot of Λm vs √c is a straight line whose intercept gives Λ°m and whose slope is −A. A depends on the solvent, temperature and type of electrolyte (charges of ions: NaCl 1-1, CaCl₂ 2-1, MgSO₄ 2-2).
Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions: Λ°m of an electrolyte = sum of limiting molar conductivities of its ions, Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋.

example.q: Find Λ°m of CaCl₂ using λ°(Ca²⁺) = 119.0 and λ°(Cl⁻) = 76.3 S cm² mol⁻¹.
steps: CaCl₂ gives 1 Ca²⁺ and 2 Cl⁻

learn.reallife: Water-treatment engineers at Indian municipal plants track conductivity to estimate total dissolved salts, using the fact that each ion contributes its own share — Kohlrausch's idea.

games.title: Dilution and conductivity
items: Conductivity of a solution decreases on dilution.
There are fewer ions per unit volume.
Molar conductivity of a solution decreases on dilution.
It increases, because Λm = κV and V grows faster than κ falls.
For strong electrolytes Λm varies linearly with √c.
Λ°m of a weak electrolyte is easily found by extrapolating the Λm vs √c plot.
The plot is not linear for weak electrolytes; Kohlrausch's law is used instead.
The constant A is the same for NaCl and MgSO₄ in water at the same temperature.
A depends on the type of electrolyte (charges on the ions).

quiz.q: What is Λ°m (in S cm² mol⁻¹) of MgCl₂? λ°(Mg²⁺) = 106.0, λ°(Cl⁻) = 76.3 S cm² mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 2 chloride ions per formula unit (gives 182.3)
steps: MgCl₂ → Mg²⁺ + 2Cl⁻
Answer: 258.6

quiz.q: What is Λ°m (in S cm² mol⁻¹) of Na₂SO₄? λ°(Na⁺) = 50.1, λ°(SO₄²⁻) = 160.0 S cm² mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Adds just one sodium ion
steps: Na₂SO₄ → 2Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻
Answer: 260.2

quiz.q: Why does the conductivity (κ) of a solution decrease on dilution?
options: The number of ions per unit volume decreases
quiz.explain: κ measures conductance of a unit volume (1 cm³); dilution leaves fewer ions in that volume.
steps: κ is the conductance of a unit volume (1 cm³) of solution.
Dilution leaves fewer ions in that volume, so κ decreases.
Answer: The number of ions per unit volume decreases
quiz.mistake: Thinks dilution reduces dissociation

quiz.q: Why does molar conductivity increase on dilution?
options: Λm = κV, and the volume V containing one mole increases more than κ decreases
quiz.explain: Although κ falls, the volume containing 1 mol of electrolyte rises faster, so their product Λm increases.
steps: Λm = κ × V, where V is the volume containing 1 mol of electrolyte.
On dilution V increases more than κ decreases, so Λm increases.
Answer: Λm = κV, and the volume V containing one mole increases more than κ decreases
quiz.mistake: Confuses molar conductivity with conductivity

quiz.q: For a strong electrolyte, a graph of Λm against √c is a straight line. What does its intercept give?
quiz.explain: From Λm = Λ°m − A√c, the intercept at √c = 0 is Λ°m and the slope is −A.
steps: Λm = Λ°m − A√c is a straight line against √c.
At √c = 0 the intercept is Λ°m; the slope is −A.
Answer: Λ°m, the limiting molar conductivity
quiz.mistake: Confuses slope and intercept

quiz.q: State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions.
options: Λ°m of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion
All ions have the same molar conductivity
quiz.explain: At infinite dilution each ion moves independently and contributes its own λ°, so Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋.
steps: At infinite dilution each ion moves independently.
So Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋: the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of the ions.
Answer: Λ°m of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Kohlrausch's law with the definition of conductivity

quiz.q: Which electrolyte would have the largest constant A in Λm = Λ°m − A√c, in water at the same temperature?
quiz.explain: A depends on the charges of the ions; MgSO₄ is a 2-2 electrolyte, giving the strongest interionic effects.
steps: A depends on the charges of the ions.
NaCl and KCl are 1-1, CaCl₂ 2-1, MgSO₄ 2-2.
Highest charges give the largest A: MgSO₄.
Answer: MgSO₄
quiz.mistake: Assumes A is the same for all electrolytes

quiz.q: Assertion (A): H⁺ has a much higher limiting molar conductivity than Na⁺. Reason (R): According to Kohlrausch's law, each ion contributes a definite share to Λ°m.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Both statements are true, but Kohlrausch's law does not explain why H⁺ moves so fast; that is due to its special proton-hopping mechanism in water.
steps: A: λ°(H⁺) 349.6 is much higher than λ°(Na⁺) 50.1. True.
R: each ion contributes a definite share to Λ°m. True.
Kohlrausch's law does not explain why H⁺ is so fast, so R is not the explanation.
Answer: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats any true statement about ions as the explanation

teach.ask: Gappu dilutes a solution: 'Why does molar conductivity go up when conductivity goes down? And what did Kohlrausch say?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Λm = κV rises as V grows, and at infinite dilution each ion contributes independently. Kohlrausch nailed it!
teach.nudge: You explained one part. What does Kohlrausch's law say about the ions at infinite dilution?

revise.summary: On dilution κ falls (fewer ions per volume) but Λm rises (Λm = κV). For strong electrolytes Λm = Λ°m − A√c, so Λ°m comes from the intercept. Kohlrausch's law: Λ°m equals the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of the ions, Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋.
focus: Effect of dilution on κ and Λm
traps: Don't say κ increases on dilution
Don't forget the stoichiometric coefficients (2 Cl⁻ in CaCl₂)

topics.title: Weak electrolytes: degree of dissociation and Ka from conductivity

learn.hook: You cannot extrapolate acetic acid's conductivity curve to zero concentration — it shoots up wildly. Kohlrausch's law offers a clever detour.
points: Weak electrolytes (e.g. CH₃COOH) have low Λm at ordinary concentrations, which rises steeply on dilution as the degree of dissociation increases.
Their Λ°m cannot be obtained by extrapolation; instead use Kohlrausch's law with strong electrolytes: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(CH₃COONa) + Λ°(HCl) − Λ°(NaCl).
Degree of dissociation at concentration c: α = Λm ÷ Λ°m.
Dissociation constant: Ka = cα² ÷ (1 − α).

example.q: Λ°m of HCl, NaCl and CH₃COONa are 425.9, 126.4 and 91.0 S cm² mol⁻¹. Find Λ°m of acetic acid.
steps: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(CH₃COONa) − Λ°(NaCl)
= 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹

learn.reallife: Vinegar (about 5% acetic acid) used in Indian pickles is a weak electrolyte; its conductivity is far lower than that of an HCl solution of the same concentration.

quiz.explain: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = 425.9 + 91.0 − 126.4 = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹: the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ contributions cancel.
quiz.mistake: Adds all three values instead of subtracting NaCl
steps: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(CH₃COONa) − Λ°(NaCl)
Answer: 390.5

quiz.q: 0.01 M acetic acid has Λm = 39.05 S cm² mol⁻¹ and Λ°m = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹. What is its degree of dissociation?

Answer: 0.1

quiz.q: For 0.01 M acetic acid with α = 0.1, Ka = n × 10⁻⁴. What is n (two decimals)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the approximation Ka = cα² (gives 1.00) when α is not negligible
steps: Ka = cα² ÷ (1 − α)
Answer: 1.11

quiz.q: Why can Λ°m of acetic acid not be found by extrapolating its Λm vs √c graph?
options: The graph is a straight line with zero slope
Acetic acid is a strong electrolyte
Acetic acid does not conduct electricity
Λm rises very steeply at low concentrations, so the curve cannot be extrapolated reliably
quiz.explain: For a weak electrolyte the degree of dissociation keeps increasing sharply on dilution, so the curve is steep near zero concentration.
steps: For a weak electrolyte, Λm rises very steeply at low concentration.
The curve cannot be extrapolated reliably to c = 0, so Kohlrausch's law is used instead.
Answer: Λm rises very steeply at low concentrations, so the curve cannot be extrapolated reliably
quiz.mistake: Assumes all electrolytes give a straight-line plot

quiz.q: Why does the molar conductivity of a weak electrolyte increase sharply on dilution?
options: Its degree of dissociation increases a lot on dilution
quiz.explain: On dilution more molecules ionise, greatly increasing the number of ions per mole.
steps: A weak electrolyte is only partly ionised.
On dilution its degree of dissociation increases a lot, so Λm rises sharply.
Answer: Its degree of dissociation increases a lot on dilution
quiz.mistake: Applies the strong-electrolyte reason (reduced interionic attraction) instead

quiz.q: Using λ°(H⁺) = 349.6 and λ°(HCOO⁻) = 54.6 S cm² mol⁻¹, what is Λ°m of formic acid (in S cm² mol⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Λ°m(HCOOH) = 349.6 + 54.6 = 404.2 S cm² mol⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the ionic conductivities
steps: Λ°m = λ°(H⁺) + λ°(HCOO⁻)
Answer: 404.2

quiz.q: A 0.001 M solution of a weak acid HA has Λm = 78.1 S cm² mol⁻¹ and Λ°m = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹. What is α?
quiz.mistake: Divides Λ°m by Λm
steps: α = Λm ÷ Λ°m
Answer: 0.2

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Kohlrausch's law helps find the dissociation constant of a weak acid from conductivity data. Reason (R): It allows Λ°m of the weak acid to be calculated from Λ°m values of strong electrolytes.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: With Λ°m known, α = Λm/Λ°m and then Ka = cα²/(1 − α); R is exactly why A works.
steps: A: Kohlrausch's law helps find Ka of a weak acid. True.
R: it gives Λ°m of the weak acid from strong electrolytes. True.
With Λ°m, α = Λm/Λ°m and Ka = cα²/(1 − α), so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see that Λ°m is the missing piece

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'How can I find how much acetic acid has dissociated just by measuring conductivity?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Get Λ°m from Kohlrausch's law, then α = Λm/Λ°m and Ka = cα²/(1 − α). Elegant!
teach.nudge: You measured Λm. What ratio gives α, and where does Λ°m come from?

revise.summary: Weak electrolytes have low Λm that rises steeply on dilution, so Λ°m cannot be found by extrapolation; Kohlrausch's law gives it, e.g. Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(CH₃COONa) + Λ°(HCl) − Λ°(NaCl). Then α = Λm/Λ°m and Ka = cα²/(1 − α).
focus: Why weak electrolytes need Kohlrausch's law
Combining Λ° values of strong electrolytes
traps: Don't extrapolate the Λm graph of a weak acid
Don't add NaCl instead of subtracting it

topics.title: Electrolysis and Faraday's laws

learn.hook: The silver-plated thali at a wedding and copper refined to 99.9% purity for wiring both depend on counting electrons — Faraday's way.
points: In electrolysis of CuSO₄ with copper electrodes, Cu²⁺ is reduced at the cathode (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu) while the copper anode dissolves (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻). This is the basis of electrorefining (impure Cu as anode) and electroplating.
In an electrolytic cell the anode is positive and the cathode is negative (opposite of a galvanic cell); oxidation is still at the anode.
Faraday's first law: mass deposited m ∝ charge Q, so m = Z × I × t, where Z is the electrochemical equivalent, I is current (A) and t is time (s).
Faraday's second law: for the same charge, masses of different substances liberated are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights (atomic mass ÷ number of electrons needed).
Charge on 1 mol of electrons = 1 F = 96487 C mol⁻¹ (≈ 96500). Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag needs 1 F per mol, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu needs 2 F, Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al needs 3 F.

example.q: A current of 2 A is passed through CuSO₄ solution for 965 s. What mass of copper is deposited? (Cu = 63.5 g mol⁻¹, F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
steps: Moles of electrons = 1930 ÷ 96500 = 0.02 mol
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so moles of Cu = 0.01 mol

learn.reallife: Electrorefining at Hindustan Copper's plants produces high-purity copper for India's power cables, and Moradabad artisans electroplate brassware with silver and nickel.

steps: Answer: 965

steps: n(Al) = 0.1 mol; n(e⁻) = 0.3 mol
Answer: 5790

quiz.explain: 1.08 g Ag means 0.01 mol e⁻ passed; Cu²⁺ needs 2e⁻, so 0.005 mol Cu = 0.3175 g.
quiz.mistake: Assumes equal moles of Ag and Cu are deposited
steps: Answer: 0.3175

quiz.q: In the electrolysis of CuSO₄ solution using copper electrodes, what happens at the anode?
quiz.explain: The copper anode is oxidised, Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, replacing the Cu²⁺ deposited at the cathode.
steps: With copper electrodes the anode itself is oxidised.
Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, so copper dissolves as Cu²⁺.
Answer: Copper dissolves as Cu²⁺ ions
quiz.mistake: Applies the inert-electrode result (O₂ at anode) to copper electrodes

quiz.q: In electrorefining of copper, which is made the anode?
quiz.explain: Impure copper dissolves at the anode, and pure copper deposits on the cathode; impurities settle as anode mud.
steps: In electrorefining, impure copper is made the anode and dissolves.
Pure copper deposits on the cathode; impurities settle as anode mud.
Answer: A block of impure copper
quiz.mistake: Swaps anode and cathode roles

quiz.q: How many faradays are needed to reduce 1 mol of MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺?
quiz.explain: Mn goes from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons per ion, so 5 F per mole.
quiz.mistake: Uses the oxidation number +7 directly
steps: Electrons gained = 5 per ion → 5 F
Answer: 5

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In an electrolytic cell the anode is the positive electrode. Reason (R): Oxidation always occurs at the anode.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Both are true. The anode is positive because it is connected to the positive terminal of the external source; the fact that oxidation happens there holds in all cells and does not explain the sign.
steps: A: in an electrolytic cell the anode is positive. True.
R: oxidation always occurs at the anode. True.
The sign comes from the external source, not from oxidation, so R is not the explanation.
Answer: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the place of oxidation decides the polarity

teach.praise: Ding! Charge = current × time, divide by F for moles of electrons, then use the electrons per ion. Shiny!
teach.nudge: You found the charge. What constant converts it into moles of electrons?

Faraday's laws: m = Z I t, and for equal charge masses are proportional to equivalent weights. 1 F ≈ 96500 C per mole of electrons.

Moles of electrons needed per ion

topics.title: Products of electrolysis

learn.hook: Electrolyse molten salt and you get sodium metal; electrolyse brine and you get hydrogen instead. Same ions, different stories.
points: Products depend on the state of the electrolyte, the nature of the electrodes (inert Pt or reactive Cu), the standard potentials of competing reactions and overpotential (extra voltage needed for some reactions, especially gas evolution).
Molten NaCl: cathode Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na(l); anode Cl⁻ → ½Cl₂(g) + e⁻.

Aqueous NaCl: at the cathode water is reduced instead of Na⁺ (E° of H₂O/H₂ = −0.83 V vs Na⁺/Na −2.71 V): H₂O + e⁻ → ½H₂ + OH⁻. At the anode Cl₂ is evolved rather than O₂ (although E° Cl₂/Cl⁻ 1.36 V > O₂ 1.23 V) because of the overpotential of oxygen. Net: NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) + ½H₂(g) + ½Cl₂(g).
Dilute H₂SO₄ (Pt electrodes): O₂ at the anode, 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ (E° 1.23 V). At higher concentration, peroxodisulphate forms: 2SO₄²⁻ → S₂O₈²⁻ + 2e⁻ (E° 1.96 V). H₂ is evolved at the cathode.

example.q: Predict the products of electrolysis of aqueous NaCl using inert electrodes.
steps: Cathode: compare Na⁺/Na (−2.71 V) with H₂O/H₂ (−0.83 V); water is reduced → H₂ + OH⁻
Anode: Cl₂ (1.36 V) vs O₂ (1.23 V); O₂ has a high overpotential, so Cl₂ forms
Na⁺ and OH⁻ remain in solution as NaOH
example.answer: H₂ at cathode, Cl₂ at anode, NaOH in solution

learn.reallife: This is the chlor-alkali process run at large plants in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu; the NaOH goes into soaps and paper, and the Cl₂ into water disinfection and PVC.

quiz.q: What is obtained at the cathode when molten NaCl is electrolysed?
quiz.explain: In the melt there is no water, so Na⁺ is the only species reduced: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na.
steps: Molten NaCl contains no water.
Only Na⁺ can be reduced at the cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na.
Answer: Sodium metal
quiz.mistake: Applies the aqueous result to the molten salt

quiz.q: Why is H₂ and not Na formed at the cathode during electrolysis of aqueous NaCl?
options: Water has a higher (less negative) reduction potential than Na⁺
Na⁺ is reduced but immediately evaporates
Na⁺ has a higher reduction potential than water
quiz.explain: E°(H₂O/H₂) = −0.83 V is less negative than E°(Na⁺/Na) = −2.71 V, so water is reduced preferentially.
steps: Compare E°: H₂O/H₂ −0.83 V vs Na⁺/Na −2.71 V.
Water's potential is less negative, so water is reduced and H₂ forms.
Answer: Water has a higher (less negative) reduction potential than Na⁺
quiz.mistake: Thinks the cation in the salt is always the one reduced

quiz.q: Why is chlorine rather than oxygen liberated at the anode in the electrolysis of brine?
options: Cl₂/Cl⁻ has a lower E° than O₂
Oxygen is not present in brine
Chloride ions are reduced at the anode
Oxygen evolution has a high overpotential
quiz.explain: Thermodynamics favours O₂ slightly (1.23 V vs 1.36 V), but the extra voltage needed for O₂ makes Cl₂ formation faster in practice.
steps: O₂ is slightly favoured thermodynamically (1.23 V vs 1.36 V).
But oxygen evolution has a high overpotential, so Cl₂ forms in practice.
Answer: Oxygen evolution has a high overpotential
quiz.mistake: Ignores overpotential and uses E° alone

quiz.q: Which substance is left in the solution after electrolysis of aqueous NaCl?
quiz.explain: Na⁺ ions remain and OH⁻ forms at the cathode, giving NaOH in solution.
steps: H₂ forms at the cathode leaving OH⁻; Na⁺ stays in solution.
Na⁺ and OH⁻ together give NaOH in solution.
Answer: Sodium hydroxide
quiz.mistake: Thinks sodium metal collects in water

quiz.q: Which product forms at the anode on electrolysis of dilute sulphuric acid with platinum electrodes?

steps: In dilute H₂SO₄, water is oxidised at the Pt anode.
2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, so oxygen is formed.
Answer: Oxygen
quiz.mistake: Gives the concentrated-acid product

quiz.q: At higher concentrations of H₂SO₄, what is the anode product?

steps: At higher concentration more sulphate ions are available.
2SO₄²⁻ → S₂O₈²⁻ + 2e⁻, giving peroxodisulphate ions.
Answer: Peroxodisulphate ions, S₂O₈²⁻
quiz.mistake: Thinks the anode product never changes with concentration

quiz.q: Aqueous CuSO₄ is electrolysed with platinum electrodes. What forms at the anode?
quiz.explain: Pt is inert, so water is oxidised to O₂; copper deposits at the cathode.
steps: Pt is inert, so it is not oxidised itself.
Water is oxidised to O₂ at the anode; Cu deposits at the cathode.
Answer: Oxygen gas
quiz.mistake: Confuses inert electrodes with copper electrodes

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The products of electrolysis can differ for the same electrolyte. Reason (R): Products depend on whether the electrolyte is molten or aqueous and on the electrode material.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Molten vs aqueous NaCl, and Pt vs Cu electrodes with CuSO₄, give different products, as R explains.

R: products depend on molten vs aqueous state and electrode material. True.

Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks electrolysis products are fixed for a salt

teach.praise: Chirp! In water, H₂O is reduced more easily than Na⁺, giving H₂; in the melt there's no water, so Na forms!

revise.summary: Electrolysis products depend on the electrolyte's state, the electrodes and competing potentials with overpotential. Molten NaCl gives Na and Cl₂; aqueous NaCl gives H₂, Cl₂ and NaOH. Dilute H₂SO₄ gives O₂ at the anode; concentrated gives S₂O₈²⁻.

remember: Aqueous NaCl: cathode H₂O + e⁻ → ½H₂ + OH⁻; anode Cl⁻ → ½Cl₂ + e⁻
traps: Don't say Na forms from aqueous NaCl
Don't forget overpotential makes Cl₂ form instead of O₂

topics.title: Batteries and fuel cells

learn.hook: The dry cell in a TV remote, the lead battery under an auto-rickshaw seat and the fuel cell that powered Apollo astronauts share the same physics but very different chemistry.
points: Primary batteries cannot be recharged. Dry (Leclanché) cell: zinc container anode (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻), carbon (graphite) rod cathode in MnO₂ + carbon, NH₄Cl/ZnCl₂ paste; cathode: MnO₂ + NH₄⁺ + e⁻ → MnO(OH) + NH₃. About 1.5 V.

Mercury cell: zinc–mercury amalgam anode, HgO + carbon paste cathode, KOH + ZnO paste electrolyte. Anode: Zn(Hg) + 2OH⁻ → ZnO(s) + H₂O + 2e⁻; cathode: HgO + H₂O + 2e⁻ → Hg(l) + 2OH⁻. About 1.35 V, constant because no ion appears in the overall reaction Zn(Hg) + HgO(s) → ZnO(s) + Hg(l). Used in hearing aids and watches.
Secondary (rechargeable) lead storage battery: Pb anode, grid of lead packed with PbO₂ as cathode, 38% H₂SO₄. Discharge: Pb(s) + PbO₂(s) + 2H₂SO₄(aq) → 2PbSO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l); charging reverses it.
Nickel–cadmium cell: Cd(s) + 2Ni(OH)₃(s) → CdO(s) + 2Ni(OH)₂(s) + H₂O(l); longer life than the lead cell but more expensive.

H₂–O₂ fuel cell (used in the Apollo programme): porous carbon electrodes with Pt/Pd catalyst in concentrated aqueous NaOH. Cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻; anode: 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻; overall 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Efficiency about 70%, versus about 40% for thermal power plants, and it is pollution free.

example.q: Why does a mercury cell give a constant voltage throughout its life, unlike a dry cell?
steps: Overall reaction: Zn(Hg) + HgO(s) → ZnO(s) + Hg(l)
No ion in solution appears in the overall reaction
So the reaction quotient, and hence E, does not change as the cell is used
example.answer: Its overall reaction involves no ions whose concentration changes, so the voltage stays about 1.35 V
