games.title: High because of a stable configuration

quiz.q: Why do transition metals have high melting points and enthalpies of atomisation?
options: Strong metallic bonding involving both (n−1)d and ns electrons
They have only s electrons for bonding
quiz.explain: Unpaired d electrons add to metallic bonding, which is strongest around the middle of a series.
steps: Transition metals have unpaired (n−1)d electrons besides ns electrons.
Both take part in strong metallic bonding, giving high melting points and enthalpies of atomisation.
Answer: Strong metallic bonding involving both (n−1)d and ns electrons
quiz.mistake: Thinks only ns electrons take part in metallic bonding

quiz.q: Which 3d metal has the lowest melting point?
quiz.explain: Zinc has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell and no unpaired d electrons, so its metallic bonding is weakest.
steps: Zinc has a full 3d¹⁰ subshell and no unpaired d electrons.
Its metallic bonding is weakest, so its melting point is lowest.
Answer: Zinc
quiz.mistake: Picks a metal from the middle of the series

quiz.q: Why are the atomic radii of Zr (160 pm) and Hf (159 pm) almost equal?
options: Hf has fewer electrons than Zr
quiz.explain: The poorly shielding 4f electrons filled before Hf cause a contraction that cancels the expected size increase.
steps: The 14 lanthanoids (4f filling) come between Zr and Hf.
Poor shielding by 4f electrons causes lanthanoid contraction, cancelling the expected size increase.
Answer: Lanthanoid contraction
quiz.mistake: Credits actinoid contraction, which affects later elements

quiz.q: Why is the second ionisation enthalpy of chromium unusually high?
options: Removing the second electron breaks the stable 3d⁵ configuration of Cr⁺
Chromium has a very large atomic radius
quiz.explain: Cr⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵, a stable half-filled subshell; removing another electron needs extra energy.
steps: Cr⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵, a stable half-filled subshell.
Removing a second electron breaks it, so the second ionisation enthalpy is high.
Answer: Removing the second electron breaks the stable 3d⁵ configuration of Cr⁺
quiz.mistake: Writes the wrong configuration for Cr⁺

quiz.q: Why is the third ionisation enthalpy of manganese unusually high?
options: Mn²⁺ has a stable half-filled 3d⁵ configuration
quiz.explain: Removing a third electron from Mn²⁺ (3d⁵) destroys the extra-stable half-filled subshell.
steps: Mn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵, half-filled and stable.
Removing a third electron destroys this, so the third ionisation enthalpy is high.
Answer: Mn²⁺ has a stable half-filled 3d⁵ configuration
quiz.mistake: Confuses half-filled with fully filled

quiz.q: How does atomic radius generally change across the 3d series?
options: It decreases sharply all the way
It decreases at first and then becomes nearly constant
quiz.explain: Increasing nuclear charge contracts the atom, but poor shielding by d electrons soon balances the effect.
steps: Nuclear charge rises across the series and pulls electrons in.
Poor shielding by added d electrons soon balances it, so radius decreases then stays nearly constant.
Answer: It decreases at first and then becomes nearly constant
quiz.mistake: Assumes the trend is as steep as in s- and p-block

quiz.q: Which property increases from titanium to copper in the 3d series?
quiz.explain: Atoms get slightly smaller while atomic mass increases, so density rises from Ti to Cu.
steps: From Ti to Cu atoms get slightly smaller while atomic mass increases.
So density increases.
Answer: Density
quiz.mistake: Assumes size also increases

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Mercury is a liquid at room temperature. Reason (R): Mercury has no unpaired d electrons, so its metallic bonding is weak.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: With a full 5d¹⁰ 6s² configuration, Hg has weak metallic bonding and a very low melting point.
steps: A: mercury is liquid at room temperature. True.
R: Hg has no unpaired d electrons, so metallic bonding is weak. True.
Weak bonding gives a very low melting point, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link unpaired electrons to metallic bond strength

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is lanthanoid contraction, and why do zirconium and hafnium look like twins?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Poor shielding by 4f electrons shrinks the 5d atoms, so Zr and Hf end up nearly the same size!
teach.nudge: You named it. Which electrons cause it, and what do they fail to do?

revise.summary: Transition metals are hard and dense with high melting points due to metallic bonding using (n−1)d and ns electrons; Zn, Cd, Hg are soft and low-melting. Radii fall then level off across a series; lanthanoid contraction makes 4d and 5d radii nearly equal. Ionisation enthalpies rise irregularly.
focus: Why transition metals have high melting points
Irregular ionisation enthalpies (Cr, Cu, Mn, Zn)
remember: High IE₂: Cr (3d⁵), Cu (3d¹⁰); high IE₃: Mn (3d⁵), Zn (3d¹⁰)
Density increases from Ti to Cu
traps: Don't say atomic radius keeps falling sharply across the series
Don't link Zr/Hf similarity to actinoid contraction

topics.title: Oxidation states and stability of higher oxidation states

learn.hook: Manganese can show every oxidation state from +2 to +7. Potassium permanganate's purple and manganese dioxide's black are just two of its many faces.
points: Transition elements show variable oxidation states because the (n−1)d and ns electrons are close in energy, so different numbers can be lost or shared; oxidation states usually differ by one.
The number of oxidation states is greatest in the middle of the 3d series: Mn shows +2 to +7. At the ends there are few: Sc mainly +3, Zn only +2.
Highest oxidation states rise up to Mn (Sc +3, Ti +4, V +5, Cr +6, Mn +7) and then fall. Low oxidation states (0, +1) appear in complexes with π-acceptor ligands like CO, e.g. Ni(CO)₄ and Fe(CO)₅.
Fluorine and oxygen stabilise high oxidation states. Oxygen does it better because it can form multiple bonds to the metal: Mn's highest fluoride is MnF₄ but its highest oxide is Mn₂O₇.

Halides: Cu(II) halides exist except the iodide, because Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻: 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂. In water, Cu⁺ disproportionates (2Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Cu) because Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy.

example.q: Find the oxidation state of Mn in KMnO₄, K₂MnO₄ and MnO₂.

learn.reallife: The Mn in the MnO₂ of a dry cell (+4) and in KMnO₄ used to disinfect village wells in India (+7) shows how one element can play many redox roles.

games.title: Compound ↔ oxidation state of the metal
Oxidation state checks
items: Scandium shows mainly the +3 oxidation state.
Losing 3d¹ 4s² gives the stable noble-gas configuration.
The highest oxidation state of Mn in its oxides is higher than in its fluorides.

quiz.q: What is the oxidation state of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇?
steps: Answer: +6
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the two Cr atoms

quiz.q: Which 3d element shows the largest number of oxidation states?
quiz.explain: Mn has the most electrons available in 3d and 4s and shows +2 to +7.
steps: Oxidation states are most numerous in the middle of the 3d series.
Mn shows every state from +2 to +7.
Answer: Manganese
quiz.mistake: Picks an element at the end of the series

quiz.q: Why is the highest oxidation state of a metal often found in its oxide rather than its fluoride?
options: Oxygen is more electronegative than fluorine
Oxygen can form multiple bonds with the metal
Fluorine cannot form bonds with metals
quiz.explain: Multiple M=O bonding lets oxygen stabilise very high oxidation states, e.g. Mn₂O₇ versus MnF₄.
steps: Oxygen can form multiple (M=O) bonds with the metal; fluorine forms only single bonds.
So oxides reach higher states: Mn₂O₇ (+7) vs MnF₄ (+4).
Answer: Oxygen can form multiple bonds with the metal
quiz.mistake: Thinks oxygen is more electronegative than fluorine

quiz.q: Why does CuI₂ not exist while CuCl₂ and CuBr₂ do?
options: Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ and is reduced to Cu(I)
Iodine is too small to bond with copper
quiz.explain: 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂: iodide is a good reducing agent.
steps: Cu²⁺ is an oxidising agent and I⁻ a good reducing agent.
2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂, so CuI₂ cannot exist.
Answer: Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ and is reduced to Cu(I)
quiz.mistake: Does not consider redox between Cu²⁺ and I⁻

quiz.q: Why is Cu⁺ unstable in aqueous solution?
options: It disproportionates to Cu²⁺ and Cu because Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy
It is oxidised by water to Cu³⁺
It has an incomplete d subshell
quiz.explain: The large hydration energy of the smaller, more highly charged Cu²⁺ more than compensates for the second ionisation enthalpy.
steps: In water, 2Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Cu.
Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy, which outweighs its second ionisation enthalpy.
Answer: It disproportionates to Cu²⁺ and Cu because Cu²⁺ has a much more negative hydration enthalpy
quiz.mistake: Ignores hydration enthalpy

quiz.q: What is the oxidation state of nickel in Ni(CO)₄?
quiz.explain: CO is a neutral ligand, so nickel is in the zero oxidation state.
quiz.mistake: Treats CO as carrying a charge
steps: CO is neutral
Answer: 0

quiz.q: Which is the highest oxidation state shown by vanadium?
quiz.explain: V has 3d³ 4s², so it can use all five electrons, as in V₂O₅.
steps: V = [Ar] 3d³ 4s²: five outer electrons.
Using all five gives +5, as in V₂O₅.
Answer: +5
quiz.mistake: Assumes all metals reach +7

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Transition elements show variable oxidation states. Reason (R): The energies of (n−1)d and ns orbitals are very close.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Because the two sets of electrons are close in energy, varying numbers can be used in bonding.
steps: A: transition elements show variable oxidation states. True.
R: (n−1)d and ns orbitals are very close in energy. True.
Close energies let varying numbers of electrons be used, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see the link to orbital energies

teach.ask: Gappu counts on his feathers: 'Why does manganese show so many oxidation states, from +2 to +7?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Mn's 3d and 4s electrons are close in energy, so it can use 2 up to all 7 of them!
teach.nudge: You said it varies. Which electrons are involved, and why can different numbers be used?

revise.summary: Transition elements show variable oxidation states because (n−1)d and ns energies are close; Mn shows the most (+2 to +7). Highest states rise to Mn then fall. Oxygen stabilises high states better than fluorine via multiple bonds. CuI₂ does not exist and Cu⁺ disproportionates in water.
focus: Which elements show most and fewest states
Role of O and F in stabilising high states
remember: Highest states: Sc +3, Ti +4, V +5, Cr +6, Mn +7
traps: Don't say fluorine stabilises higher states than oxygen
Don't give Cr +12 in K₂Cr₂O₇; divide by two Cr atoms

topics.title: Electrode potentials and chemical reactivity

learn.hook: Most 3d metals fizz in dilute acid, but copper sits calmly in it. The answer lies in a positive standard electrode potential and the energy accounting behind it.
points: E°(M²⁺/M) is generally negative across the 3d series (e.g. Mn −1.18, Fe −0.44, Ni −0.25, Zn −0.76 V), so these metals liberate H₂ from dilute acids.

Copper is unique with E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V: its high enthalpy of atomisation and ionisation enthalpies are not balanced by its hydration enthalpy, so it does not liberate H₂ from acids (only oxidising acids like HNO₃ react).
Values for Mn, Ni and Zn are more negative than the general trend: Mn²⁺ (d⁵) and Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰) are extra stable, and Ni²⁺ has a very negative hydration enthalpy.

E°(M³⁺/M²⁺): Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ = +1.57 V and Co³⁺/Co²⁺ = +1.97 V are high, so Mn³⁺ and Co³⁺ are strong oxidising agents. The comparatively low value for Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ (+0.77 V) reflects the stability of Fe³⁺ (d⁵). Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ = −0.41 V, so Cr²⁺ is a strong reducing agent (it becomes stable d³).
Chemical reactivity: apart from copper, 3d metals are fairly reactive and are oxidised by 1 M H⁺, although some (like Ti and V) are passive due to protective oxide films.

example.q: Cr²⁺ and Mn³⁺ are both d⁴. Why is Cr²⁺ reducing while Mn³⁺ is oxidising?
steps: Cr²⁺ (d⁴) → Cr³⁺ (d³): loses an electron to reach the stable half-filled t₂g³ arrangement — acts as a reducing agent
Mn³⁺ (d⁴) → Mn²⁺ (d⁵): gains an electron to reach the extra-stable half-filled d⁵ — acts as an oxidising agent
This matches E°: Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ −0.41 V, Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ +1.57 V
example.answer: Cr²⁺ is oxidised to stable d³; Mn³⁺ is reduced to stable d⁵

learn.reallife: Copper does not liberate hydrogen from dilute non-oxidising acids, but in air sour foods slowly attack it; that is why traditional copper and brass cookware in Indian kitchens is lined with tin (kalai) before acidic dishes are cooked in it.

games.title: Oxidising or reducing agent in water?

quiz.q: Why does copper not liberate hydrogen from dilute HCl?
options: Copper has a very negative E°
Copper forms a protective oxide in HCl
quiz.explain: A positive reduction potential means Cu is a weaker reducing agent than H₂, so it cannot reduce H⁺.
steps: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V is positive, above H⁺/H₂ (0.00 V).
So copper is a weaker reducing agent than H₂ and cannot reduce H⁺.
Answer: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) is positive (+0.34 V)
quiz.mistake: Thinks all metals displace hydrogen

quiz.q: What is the main reason for the positive E°(Cu²⁺/Cu)?
options: Cu has a very low enthalpy of atomisation
Cu²⁺ is not hydrated in water
High enthalpy of atomisation and ionisation of Cu are not balanced by its hydration enthalpy
quiz.explain: Turning solid Cu into hydrated Cu²⁺ costs more energy than hydration returns.
steps: Forming Cu²⁺(aq) from Cu(s) needs atomisation and ionisation energy.
For Cu these are high and not balanced by its hydration enthalpy, so E° is positive.
Answer: High enthalpy of atomisation and ionisation of Cu are not balanced by its hydration enthalpy
quiz.mistake: Ignores the energy cycle behind E°

quiz.q: Why is Mn³⁺ a strong oxidising agent?
options: It readily loses an electron to form d³
It has a full d¹⁰ configuration
It readily gains an electron to form the stable d⁵ Mn²⁺
quiz.explain: E°(Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺) = +1.57 V: reduction to half-filled d⁵ Mn²⁺ is highly favourable.
steps: E°(Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺) = +1.57 V is high.
Mn³⁺ (d⁴) gains an electron to form stable half-filled d⁵ Mn²⁺, so it oxidises others.
Answer: It readily gains an electron to form the stable d⁵ Mn²⁺
quiz.mistake: Confuses oxidising with reducing behaviour

quiz.q: Why is Cr²⁺ a strong reducing agent?
options: It is reduced to Cr metal easily
It is oxidised to Cr³⁺, which has a stable t₂g³ (d³) configuration
quiz.explain: E°(Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺) = −0.41 V; Cr²⁺ gives up an electron to become stable Cr³⁺.
steps: Cr²⁺ (d⁴) loses an electron to form stable Cr³⁺ (t₂g³, d³), so it is a reducing agent.
Answer: It is oxidised to Cr³⁺, which has a stable t₂g³ (d³) configuration
quiz.mistake: Thinks d⁴ ions always behave the same

quiz.q: Why is E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) comparatively low among the M³⁺/M²⁺ couples of the 3d series?
options: Iron does not form a +3 ion
Fe³⁺ has the extra-stable d⁵ configuration
quiz.explain: Because Fe³⁺ (d⁵) is stable, it is less eager to be reduced, so the potential is lower than for Mn or Co.
steps: Fe³⁺ is d⁵, extra stable.
It is less eager to be reduced, so E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V is comparatively low.
Answer: Fe³⁺ has the extra-stable d⁵ configuration
quiz.mistake: Writes the wrong d-count for Fe³⁺

quiz.q: Which ion is the strongest oxidising agent in aqueous solution? E°: Co³⁺/Co²⁺ +1.97 V, Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ +1.57 V, Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V, Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ −0.41 V.
quiz.explain: The highest reduction potential (+1.97 V) means Co³⁺ is most easily reduced.
steps: Strongest oxidising agent = highest reduction potential.
Co³⁺/Co²⁺ +1.97 V is highest.
Answer: Co³⁺
quiz.mistake: Picks the most negative value

quiz.q: Why is E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) more negative than expected from the general trend?
options: Zinc has a high enthalpy of atomisation
Zn²⁺ has a half-filled d subshell
Zn²⁺ has a stable, completely filled 3d¹⁰ configuration
quiz.explain: The stability of d¹⁰ Zn²⁺ makes oxidation of Zn especially favourable.
steps: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, completely filled and stable.
This makes oxidation of Zn especially favourable, giving a more negative E°.
Answer: Zn²⁺ has a stable, completely filled 3d¹⁰ configuration
quiz.mistake: Confuses full and half-filled stability

quiz.q: Assertion (A): E°(Mn²⁺/Mn) is more negative than expected from the trend across the 3d series. Reason (R): Mn²⁺ has a stable half-filled d⁵ configuration.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The stability of d⁵ Mn²⁺ makes its formation from Mn more favourable, giving a more negative E°.
steps: A: E°(Mn²⁺/Mn) is more negative than the trend. True.
R: Mn²⁺ has a stable half-filled d⁵ configuration. True.
d⁵ stability favours forming Mn²⁺, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link configuration stability to E°

teach.ask: Gappu dips a copper coin in acid: 'Why doesn't copper fizz like zinc?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Copper's E° is positive because its atomisation and ionisation costs aren't paid back by hydration. No fizz!
teach.nudge: What is the sign of copper's E°, and which energy terms explain it?

revise.summary: E°(M²⁺/M) is generally negative for 3d metals, so they liberate H₂ from acids; copper (+0.34 V) does not because its atomisation and ionisation enthalpies are not balanced by hydration. Mn, Ni, Zn are more negative than the trend. Mn³⁺ and Co³⁺ are strong oxidants; Cr²⁺ is a strong reductant.
focus: Role of d⁵, d³ and d¹⁰ stability
remember: Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ +1.57 V; Co³⁺/Co²⁺ +1.97 V; Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V; Cr³⁺/Cr²⁺ −0.41 V
Cr²⁺ → Cr³⁺ (d³): reducing; Mn³⁺ → Mn²⁺ (d⁵): oxidising
traps: Don't call Cr²⁺ an oxidising agent
Don't say copper displaces H₂ from dilute HCl

topics.title: Magnetic properties and coloured ions

learn.hook: Copper sulphate crystals are blue, potassium permanganate is purple and zinc sulphate is white. Count the unpaired d electrons and much of the mystery melts away.
points: Substances with unpaired electrons are paramagnetic (attracted by a magnetic field); those with all electrons paired are diamagnetic (weakly repelled).
Spin-only magnetic moment: μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons. n = 1 → 1.73, 2 → 2.83, 3 → 3.87, 4 → 4.90, 5 → 5.92 BM.
In a complex or hydrated ion, the d orbitals split into groups of different energy. An electron absorbs visible light to jump between them (a d–d transition), and we see the complementary colour.

Ions with d⁰ or d¹⁰ configurations have no d–d transitions and are colourless in water: Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Cu⁺ and Zn²⁺. Coloured examples: Ti³⁺ purple, V³⁺ green, Cr³⁺ violet, Mn²⁺ pink, Fe²⁺ green, Fe³⁺ yellow, Co²⁺ pink, Ni²⁺ green, Cu²⁺ blue.

example.q: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Fe²⁺ (Z of Fe = 26).
steps: Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶
Four unpaired electrons (↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑)

learn.reallife: MRI scanners at AIIMS use contrast agents built around strongly paramagnetic ions (gadolinium complexes), the same idea of unpaired electrons responding to a magnetic field.

games.title: Coloured or colourless in aqueous solution?

quiz.q: What is the spin-only magnetic moment (in BM) of Mn²⁺ (Z of Mn = 25)?
quiz.explain: Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵ with 5 unpaired electrons: μ = √(5 × 7) = √35 = 5.92 BM.
quiz.mistake: Counts 4 unpaired electrons
steps: Mn²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁵, n = 5
Answer: 5.92

quiz.q: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment (in BM) of Cr³⁺ (Z of Cr = 24).
quiz.explain: Cr³⁺ is 3d³ with 3 unpaired electrons: μ = √15 = 3.87 BM.
quiz.mistake: Removes electrons from 3d before 4s
steps: Cr³⁺: [Ar] 3d³, n = 3
Answer: 3.87

quiz.q: A divalent ion of the 3d series has a magnetic moment of 2.83 BM. How many unpaired electrons does it have?
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the magnitude without solving
steps: Answer: 2

quiz.q: Why is Zn²⁺ colourless in aqueous solution?
options: It has a completely filled 3d¹⁰ configuration, so no d–d transition is possible
quiz.explain: A full d subshell leaves no vacancy for an electron to jump into.
steps: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰: all d orbitals full.
No vacancy means no d–d transition, so it absorbs no visible light and is colourless.
Answer: It has a completely filled 3d¹⁰ configuration, so no d–d transition is possible
quiz.mistake: Thinks any transition-metal ion must be coloured

quiz.q: Which ion is diamagnetic?
quiz.explain: Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰ with all electrons paired.
steps: Cu⁺ = [Ar] 3d¹⁰: all electrons paired.
No unpaired electrons means diamagnetic; Cu²⁺, Fe³⁺ and Ni²⁺ have unpaired electrons.
Answer: Cu⁺
quiz.mistake: Assumes Cu⁺ has the same configuration as Cu²⁺

quiz.q: What causes the colour of most transition-metal ions in solution?
options: Absorption of visible light that promotes a d electron to a higher-energy d orbital
Reflection of light by unpaired electrons
Presence of a full d subshell
Emission of light by the solvent
quiz.explain: d–d transitions absorb certain wavelengths, and the complementary colour is observed.
steps: In a complex the d orbitals split into groups of different energy.
A d electron absorbs visible light to jump up (d–d transition); we see the complementary colour.
Answer: Absorption of visible light that promotes a d electron to a higher-energy d orbital
quiz.mistake: Thinks we see the colour that is absorbed

quiz.q: Which ion has the highest spin-only magnetic moment: Ti³⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe³⁺ or Ni²⁺?
quiz.explain: Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵ with five unpaired electrons; Ti³⁺ has 1, Cu²⁺ 1 and Ni²⁺ 2.
steps: Unpaired electrons: Ti³⁺ (d¹) 1, Cu²⁺ (d⁹) 1, Ni²⁺ (d⁸) 2, Fe³⁺ (d⁵) 5.
μ = √[n(n + 2)] rises with n, so Fe³⁺ (5.92 BM) is highest.
Answer: Fe³⁺
quiz.mistake: Counts electrons for the neutral atom

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Sc³⁺ compounds are colourless. Reason (R): Sc³⁺ has no electrons in its 3d orbitals.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: A d⁰ ion has no d electrons to undergo d–d transitions, so it is colourless.
steps: A: Sc³⁺ compounds are colourless. True.
R: Sc³⁺ has no 3d electrons. True.
With no d electrons, no d–d transition is possible, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect d⁰ with absence of colour

teach.ask: Gappu stares at a magnet: 'How can I predict whether an ion is paramagnetic and how strong it is?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Count unpaired electrons and use μ = √[n(n+2)] BM. More unpaired, more magnetic!
teach.nudge: What do you need to count, and which formula turns it into a magnetic moment?

revise.summary: Substances with unpaired electrons are paramagnetic; spin-only μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM. Transition-metal ions are coloured because d–d transitions absorb visible light and we see the complementary colour. d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions (Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Cu⁺, Zn²⁺) are colourless.
remember: Cu²⁺ blue, Ni²⁺ green, Mn²⁺ pink, Ti³⁺ purple
traps: Don't count paired electrons in n
Don't say d¹⁰ ions are coloured

topics.title: Complexes, catalysts, interstitial compounds and alloys

learn.hook: The urea made in Indian fertiliser plants starts with ammonia from the iron-catalysed Haber process, and sulphuric acid plants depend on vanadium pentoxide. Transition metals are chemistry's matchmakers.
points: Transition metals form many complexes, e.g. [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ and [PtCl₄]²⁻, because their ions are small, highly charged and have vacant d orbitals of suitable energy to accept lone pairs from ligands.

They are good catalysts because they can show multiple oxidation states, form complexes with reactants, and (as solids) adsorb reactants on their surface. Examples: V₂O₅ in the Contact process (SO₂ → SO₃), finely divided Fe in the Haber process, Ni in hydrogenation of oils.
Fe³⁺ catalyses 2I⁻ + S₂O₈²⁻ → I₂ + 2SO₄²⁻ via 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂ and then 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻.

Interstitial compounds form when small atoms (H, C, N) are trapped in the metal lattice, e.g. TiC, Mn₄N, Fe₃H, VH₀.₅₆, TiH₁.₇. They are usually non-stoichiometric, have higher melting points than the pure metals, are very hard, retain metallic conductivity and are chemically inert.
Alloys form readily because transition metals have similar atomic radii (within about 15%), so one can replace another in the lattice: steels with Cr, V, W, Mo, Mn; brass (Cu + Zn); bronze (Cu + Sn).

example.q: Explain how Fe³⁺ catalyses the reaction between iodide and persulphate ions.
steps: Step 1: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂
Step 2: 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻
Fe³⁺ is regenerated; both steps involve oppositely charged ions, unlike the slow direct reaction between two anions
example.answer: Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ shuttles electrons, using its variable oxidation states

learn.reallife: Vegetable ghee (vanaspati) is made by hydrogenating vegetable oils over a nickel catalyst, and the brass of a kitchen lota is an alloy of copper and zinc.

games.title: Interstitial compounds and alloys

Interstitial compounds have lower melting points than the pure metals.

Brass is an alloy of copper and tin.
Brass is copper + zinc; bronze is copper + tin.
Transition metals form alloys easily because their atomic radii are similar.
Atoms within about 15% in size can substitute for one another.
TiC and Fe₃H are examples of interstitial compounds.
Small C and H atoms sit in the holes of the metal lattice.

quiz.q: Why do transition metal ions form a large number of complexes?
options: They have only filled d orbitals
Small size, high charge and availability of vacant d orbitals
quiz.explain: These features let them attract and accept electron pairs from ligands.
steps: Transition metal ions are small and highly charged.
They have vacant d orbitals of suitable energy to accept lone pairs from ligands.
Answer: Small size, high charge and availability of vacant d orbitals
quiz.mistake: Thinks large ions form complexes more easily

quiz.q: Which catalyst is used in the Contact process for making sulphuric acid?
quiz.explain: V₂O₅ catalyses the oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃.
steps: In the Contact process SO₂ is oxidised to SO₃.
The catalyst is V₂O₅.
Answer: V₂O₅
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Haber process catalyst

quiz.q: What is the main reason transition metals and their compounds act as good catalysts?
options: They have very low melting points
They are always in the zero oxidation state
Their ability to show multiple oxidation states and form complexes
quiz.explain: Variable oxidation states let them form and break intermediates; surfaces also adsorb reactants.
steps: Transition metals can change oxidation state easily, forming and breaking intermediates.
They also form complexes with reactants.
Answer: Their ability to show multiple oxidation states and form complexes
quiz.mistake: Ascribes catalysis to colour or melting point

quiz.q: In the Fe³⁺-catalysed reaction of I⁻ with S₂O₈²⁻, what is the role of Fe²⁺?
options: It reduces S₂O₈²⁻ and is oxidised back to Fe³⁺
quiz.explain: 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻ regenerates the catalyst.
steps: Step 2: 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻.
Fe²⁺ reduces persulphate and is oxidised back to Fe³⁺, regenerating the catalyst.
Answer: It reduces S₂O₈²⁻ and is oxidised back to Fe³⁺
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two steps

quiz.q: Which statement about interstitial compounds is correct?
options: They are very hard and have high melting points
They are poor conductors of electricity
quiz.explain: Small atoms in the lattice holes make the solid harder and higher melting, while metallic conductivity stays.
steps: Small atoms trapped in the metal lattice make the solid harder.
Interstitial compounds are very hard with high melting points, and keep metallic conductivity.
Answer: They are very hard and have high melting points
quiz.mistake: Thinks they behave like ionic salts

quiz.q: Which of these is an interstitial compound?
quiz.explain: In TiC, small carbon atoms occupy the holes of the titanium lattice.
steps: Interstitial compounds have small atoms (H, C, N) in metal lattice holes.
In TiC, carbon sits in the titanium lattice.
Answer: TiC
quiz.mistake: Picks an ordinary ionic or covalent compound

quiz.q: Why do transition metals readily form alloys with one another?
options: They do not form metallic bonds
Their atomic radii are very similar
quiz.explain: Atoms of similar size (within about 15%) can replace each other in the crystal lattice.
steps: Transition metal atomic radii are very similar (within about 15%).
So one atom can replace another in the lattice, forming alloys.
Answer: Their atomic radii are very similar
quiz.mistake: Thinks alloy formation needs very different atoms

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Finely divided iron is used as a catalyst in the Haber process. Reason (R): Transition metals provide a surface on which reactant molecules can be adsorbed.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Finely divided iron has a large surface area that adsorbs N₂ and H₂, weakening their bonds and speeding up the reaction.
steps: A: finely divided iron catalyses the Haber process. True.
R: transition metals provide a surface for adsorbing reactants. True.
Adsorption on the large iron surface speeds the reaction, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link catalysis to surface adsorption

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why are transition metals such good catalysts?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Variable oxidation states, complex formation and large surfaces make them great catalysts!
teach.nudge: You said they're good catalysts. What property of their oxidation states helps?

revise.summary: Transition metals form many complexes (small, highly charged ions with vacant d orbitals) and are good catalysts (variable oxidation states, complex formation, surface adsorption), e.g. V₂O₅, Fe, Ni. Interstitial compounds like TiC are hard and high-melting. Similar radii let them form alloys.
focus: Why they are good catalysts, with examples
remember: V₂O₅: Contact process; Fe: Haber process; Ni: hydrogenation
Interstitial: TiC, Mn₄N, Fe₃H; hard, high melting, conducting
Brass = Cu + Zn; bronze = Cu + Sn
traps: Don't say interstitial compounds are poor conductors
Don't say alloys form because radii differ greatly

topics.title: Oxides, oxoanions and potassium dichromate

learn.hook: The orange crystals used in old breath-analyser tests and as a primary standard in volumetric analysis are potassium dichromate. Turn the solution alkaline and it switches to yellow chromate.
points: Oxides: the higher the oxidation state, the more acidic the oxide. Mn₂O₇ (+7, a covalent green oil) and CrO₃ (+6) are acidic; V₂O₅ is amphoteric though mainly acidic; Cr₂O₃ is amphoteric; CrO and MnO are basic.

Preparation of K₂Cr₂O₇ from chromite ore: 4FeCr₂O₄ + 8Na₂CO₃ + 7O₂ → 8Na₂CrO₄ + 2Fe₂O₃ + 8CO₂ (fusion in air). Acidify: 2Na₂CrO₄ + 2H⁺ → Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2Na⁺ + H₂O. Then Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2KCl → K₂Cr₂O₇ + 2NaCl (K₂Cr₂O₇ is less soluble and crystallises as orange crystals).
Chromate and dichromate interconvert with pH: 2CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) + H₂O; Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 2OH⁻ → 2CrO₄²⁻ + H₂O.
Structures: chromate is tetrahedral; dichromate is two tetrahedra sharing one corner, with a Cr–O–Cr bond angle of 126°.

In acid, dichromate is a strong oxidant: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O (E° = 1.33 V). It oxidises I⁻ to I₂, Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, H₂S to S and Sn²⁺ to Sn⁴⁺: e.g. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. K₂Cr₂O₇ is used as a primary standard in volumetric analysis.

example.q: Balance the ionic equation for acidified dichromate oxidising iodide.
steps: Reduction: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O
Oxidation: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻; multiply by 3
Add: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6I⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3I₂ + 7H₂O

learn.reallife: Analytical labs use K₂Cr₂O₇ as a primary standard to estimate iron(II) salts such as Mohr's salt; leather tanneries in Kanpur and Chennai use chromium(III) salts derived from dichromate.

games.title: Making K₂Cr₂O₇ from chromite ore
items: Fuse chromite (FeCr₂O₄) with Na₂CO₃ in air
Acidify to convert chromate into sodium dichromate
Add KCl to the Na₂Cr₂O₇ solution
Orange crystals of K₂Cr₂O₇ separate out

games.title: Acidic, amphoteric or basic oxide?

quiz.q: What happens when an alkali is added to an orange solution of potassium dichromate?
options: It turns purple as permanganate forms
It turns yellow as chromate ions form
It turns green as Cr³⁺ forms
quiz.explain: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 2OH⁻ → 2CrO₄²⁻ + H₂O; chromate is yellow.
steps: In alkali: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 2OH⁻ → 2CrO₄²⁻ + H₂O.
Chromate is yellow, so the orange solution turns yellow.
Answer: It turns yellow as chromate ions form
quiz.mistake: Confuses a pH change with a redox change

quiz.q: Which is the correct balanced equation for the oxidation of Fe²⁺ by acidified dichromate?
quiz.explain: Each Cr gains 3 electrons (6 for two Cr), so 6 Fe²⁺ are oxidised; charges and atoms balance.
steps: Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ gains 6 e⁻; each Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ loses 1 e⁻, so 6 Fe²⁺.
Balance O with 7H₂O and H with 14H⁺: charge +24 on each side.
So Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O.
Answer: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O
quiz.mistake: Forgets that two Cr atoms each gain 3 electrons

quiz.q: What is the Cr–O–Cr bond angle in the dichromate ion?
quiz.explain: Two CrO₄ tetrahedra share one oxygen at the corner, with a Cr–O–Cr angle of 126°.
steps: Dichromate is two CrO₄ tetrahedra sharing one corner oxygen.
The Cr–O–Cr bond angle is 126°.
Answer: 126°
quiz.mistake: Assumes a linear bridge

quiz.q: Why is K₂Cr₂O₇ made from Na₂Cr₂O₇ by adding KCl?
options: K₂Cr₂O₇ is less soluble, so it crystallises out
quiz.explain: Sodium dichromate is more soluble; the potassium salt separates as orange crystals.
steps: Na₂Cr₂O₇ + 2KCl → K₂Cr₂O₇ + 2NaCl.
K₂Cr₂O₇ is less soluble, so it crystallises out as orange crystals.
Answer: K₂Cr₂O₇ is less soluble, so it crystallises out
quiz.mistake: Thinks a redox reaction takes place

quiz.q: Which oxide is the most acidic?
quiz.explain: Mn is in its highest oxidation state (+7); acidity increases with oxidation state.
steps: Acidity of oxides rises with the metal's oxidation state.
Mn₂O₇ has Mn at +7, the highest here.
Answer: Mn₂O₇
quiz.mistake: Thinks lower oxidation states give acidic oxides

quiz.q: How many electrons are gained by one dichromate ion when it is reduced to Cr³⁺ in acid?
quiz.explain: Each of the two Cr atoms goes from +6 to +3, gaining 3 electrons: total 6.
quiz.mistake: Counts electrons for one Cr only
steps: Cr: +6 → +3, gain 3 e⁻ per Cr
2 Cr → 6 e⁻
Answer: 6

quiz.q: What happens when H₂S is passed through acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ solution?
options: SO₂ is evolved and the solution turns yellow
Sulphur is precipitated and the solution turns green
quiz.explain: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3H₂S + 8H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3S + 7H₂O; Cr³⁺ is green and S is a pale yellow precipitate.
steps: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3H₂S + 8H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3S + 7H₂O.
Sulphur precipitates and green Cr³⁺ forms.
Answer: Sulphur is precipitated and the solution turns green
quiz.mistake: Assumes chromium is reduced to the metal

quiz.q: Assertion (A): An orange dichromate solution turns yellow on adding NaOH. Reason (R): The oxidation state of chromium changes from +6 to +3.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: The colour change is due to dichromate converting to chromate; Cr stays +6 in both, so R is false.
steps: A: orange dichromate turns yellow with NaOH. True.
R: Cr changes from +6 to +3. False: Cr is +6 in both dichromate and chromate.
So A is true, R is false.
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Thinks every colour change is a redox change

teach.ask: Gappu watches a colour change: 'Why does dichromate go yellow in alkali and orange again in acid?'
teach.praise: Chirp! In alkali dichromate becomes yellow chromate, in acid it goes back to orange dichromate — Cr stays +6!
teach.nudge: Which two ions are involved, and what controls which one is present?

revise.summary: Higher oxidation states give more acidic oxides (Mn₂O₇, CrO₃). K₂Cr₂O₇ is made from chromite via Na₂CrO₄ and Na₂Cr₂O₇. Chromate (yellow) and dichromate (orange) interconvert with pH. Acidified dichromate (E° 1.33 V) oxidises I⁻, Fe²⁺, H₂S and Sn²⁺ and is a primary standard.
focus: Acidity of oxides vs oxidation state
traps: Don't say Cr changes oxidation state in chromate ⇌ dichromate
Don't balance with 3 Fe²⁺; it needs 6

topics.title: Potassium permanganate

learn.hook: A pinch of 'lal dawa' turns a bucket of water pink and kills germs. That's potassium permanganate, one of the most versatile oxidising agents in the lab.
points: Preparation: fuse MnO₂ (pyrolusite) with KOH and an oxidant (like KNO₃ or air) to form dark green K₂MnO₄: 2MnO₂ + 4KOH + O₂ → 2K₂MnO₄ + 2H₂O. In neutral or acidic solution, manganate disproportionates: 3MnO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ → 2MnO₄⁻ + MnO₂ + 2H₂O.

Commercially, MnO₂ is fused with alkali and oxidised to manganate (MnO₄²⁻), which is then oxidised electrolytically in alkaline solution to permanganate (MnO₄⁻). In the lab, Mn²⁺ can be oxidised by peroxodisulphate to permanganate.
Structures: both manganate (green, paramagnetic with one unpaired electron) and permanganate (purple, diamagnetic) are tetrahedral.

Acidic medium: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (E° = 1.52 V). It oxidises I⁻ to I₂, Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, oxalate to CO₂, H₂S to S, sulphite to sulphate and nitrite to nitrate. Dilute H₂SO₄ (not HCl) is used, since HCl would be oxidised to Cl₂.

Neutral or faintly alkaline medium: MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻. Iodide is oxidised to iodate (2MnO₄⁻ + H₂O + I⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 2OH⁻ + IO₃⁻), thiosulphate to sulphate, and Mn²⁺ to MnO₂ (in the presence of zinc sulphate or zinc oxide).

example.q: Balance the reaction of acidified permanganate with oxalate ions.
steps: Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (×2)
Oxidation: C₂O₄²⁻ → 2CO₂ + 2e⁻ (×5)
Add: 2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O + 10CO₂

learn.reallife: Indian health workers have long used KMnO₄ ('lal dawa') to disinfect wells and rinse vegetables; in CBSE titrations it acts as its own indicator, turning pink at the end point.

With S₂O₃²⁻ in neutral/faintly alkaline medium

quiz.q: How many electrons does MnO₄⁻ gain when it is reduced in acidic medium?
quiz.explain: Mn goes from +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺, a gain of 5 electrons.
quiz.mistake: Uses the neutral-medium change to MnO₂ (3 electrons)
steps: Electrons gained = 5
Answer: 5

quiz.q: What is the product of reduction of MnO₄⁻ in neutral or faintly alkaline medium?
quiz.explain: MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻; Mn goes from +7 to +4.
steps: In neutral or faintly alkaline medium: MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O + 3e⁻ → MnO₂ + 4OH⁻.
Mn goes from +7 to +4, forming MnO₂.
Answer: MnO₂
quiz.mistake: Gives the acidic-medium product

quiz.q: Why is dilute H₂SO₄ and not HCl used to acidify KMnO₄ in titrations?
options: HCl is too weak an acid
KMnO₄ would oxidise HCl to chlorine
quiz.explain: Permanganate is a strong enough oxidant to oxidise Cl⁻ to Cl₂, which would consume extra titrant.

That would use up extra titrant, so dilute H₂SO₄ is used instead of HCl.
Answer: KMnO₄ would oxidise HCl to chlorine
quiz.mistake: Thinks the choice is about acid strength

quiz.q: Which is the correctly balanced equation for MnO₄⁻ oxidising Fe²⁺ in acid?
quiz.explain: MnO₄⁻ gains 5 e⁻ and each Fe²⁺ loses 1, so 5 Fe²⁺ react per MnO₄⁻; charges balance (+17 on each side).
steps: MnO₄⁻ gains 5 e⁻ (→ Mn²⁺); each Fe²⁺ loses 1 e⁻, so 5 Fe²⁺.
Balance O with 4H₂O and H with 8H⁺; charge is +17 on both sides.
Answer: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O

quiz.q: What is the shape and magnetic nature of the permanganate ion?
quiz.explain: In MnO₄⁻, Mn(+7) is d⁰ with no unpaired electrons, and the ion is tetrahedral.
steps: In MnO₄⁻, Mn is +7 (d⁰), so no unpaired electrons: diamagnetic.
The ion is tetrahedral.
Answer: Tetrahedral and diamagnetic
quiz.mistake: Confuses permanganate with manganate

quiz.q: What is formed when acidified KMnO₄ reacts with a nitrite?
quiz.explain: 5NO₂⁻ + 2MnO₄⁻ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5NO₃⁻ + 3H₂O.
steps: Acidified KMnO₄ oxidises nitrite to nitrate.
5NO₂⁻ + 2MnO₄⁻ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5NO₃⁻ + 3H₂O.
Answer: Nitrate ions
quiz.mistake: Thinks nitrite is reduced

quiz.q: In neutral or faintly alkaline solution, KMnO₄ oxidises iodide to:
quiz.explain: 2MnO₄⁻ + H₂O + I⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 2OH⁻ + IO₃⁻; in acid the product would be I₂.
steps: In neutral or faintly alkaline medium iodide is oxidised further than in acid.
2MnO₄⁻ + H₂O + I⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 2OH⁻ + IO₃⁻, giving iodate.
Answer: iodate (IO₃⁻)
quiz.mistake: Gives the acidic-medium product

quiz.q: Assertion (A): No separate indicator is needed in titrations with KMnO₄. Reason (R): The intensely coloured MnO₄⁻ gives a pink colour as soon as it is in slight excess, while Mn²⁺ is nearly colourless.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: At the end point the first excess drop of purple permanganate tints the solution pink, so it acts as a self-indicator.
steps: A: no separate indicator is needed in KMnO₄ titrations. True.
R: the first slight excess of purple MnO₄⁻ turns the solution pink; Mn²⁺ is nearly colourless. True.
KMnO₄ acts as a self-indicator, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

teach.nudge: What product forms in acid, and what forms in neutral solution?

revise.summary: KMnO₄ is made by fusing MnO₂ with KOH and an oxidant to green K₂MnO₄, then oxidising (or disproportionating) it to purple KMnO₄. Manganate (paramagnetic) and permanganate (diamagnetic) are tetrahedral. In acid MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ (5e⁻); in neutral or alkaline medium MnO₄⁻ → MnO₂ (3e⁻).

Reactions in acidic vs neutral/alkaline medium
