Don't say iodide gives I₂ in neutral medium; it gives iodate

topics.title: The lanthanoids

learn.hook: The flint in a gas lighter and the rare-earth magnets in electric vehicle motors use lanthanoids — and India's Indian Rare Earths Ltd mines them from the monazite sands of Kerala.
points: Lanthanoids are the 14 elements Ce (58) to Lu (71) after lanthanum, filling 4f orbitals. General configuration 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s²; all Ln³⁺ ions are 4fⁿ (n = 1 for Ce³⁺ to 14 for Lu³⁺).

Lanthanoid contraction: atomic and ionic radii decrease steadily from La to Lu because 4f electrons shield one another imperfectly, so effective nuclear charge rises. Consequences: 4d and 5d elements of a group have similar radii (Zr/Hf), lanthanoids are hard to separate, and basicity of Ln(OH)₃ decreases from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃.

+3 is the characteristic oxidation state. Ce⁴⁺ (4f⁰) is a strong oxidant (E°(Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺) = +1.74 V) and Tb⁴⁺ (4f⁷) is also an oxidant; Eu²⁺ (4f⁷) and Yb²⁺ (4f¹⁴) are strong reducing agents. Stability comes from empty, half-filled or filled f subshells.

Lanthanoids are silvery-white soft metals that tarnish in air. Early members are about as reactive as calcium. They liberate H₂ from dilute acids, burn in halogens to form halides, react with water to form Ln(OH)₃ and H₂, form carbides (Ln₃C, Ln₂C₃, LnC₂) with carbon at 2773 K, and give LnN with N₂ on heating.

Uses: misch metal (about 95% lanthanoid metal and 5% iron, with traces of S, C, Ca and Al) in magnesium alloys for bullets, shells and lighter flints; mixed oxides as cracking catalysts; some oxides as phosphors.

example.q: Why is Ce⁴⁺ a good oxidising agent while Eu²⁺ is a good reducing agent?
steps: Ce⁴⁺ is 4f⁰ but the common state is +3, so Ce⁴⁺ tends to gain an electron: Ce⁴⁺ + e⁻ → Ce³⁺ (E° = +1.74 V)
Eu²⁺ is 4f⁷ (half-filled) but it tends to reach the common +3 state by losing an electron
Both revert to the characteristic +3 state
example.answer: Ce⁴⁺ is reduced to Ce³⁺; Eu²⁺ is oxidised to Eu³⁺

learn.reallife: Kerala's beach sands contain monazite; IREL processes it for rare earths now needed for the magnets in wind turbines and EV motors under India's clean-energy push.

quiz.q: What is the most common oxidation state of the lanthanoids?
quiz.explain: All lanthanoids show +3; +2 and +4 occur only where they give f⁰, f⁷ or f¹⁴.
steps: All lanthanoids show +3.
+2 and +4 occur only when they give f⁰, f⁷ or f¹⁴.
Answer: +3
quiz.mistake: Assumes they behave like transition metals with many states

quiz.q: What is the main cause of lanthanoid contraction?
options: Imperfect shielding of one 4f electron by another
Increase in the number of electron shells
quiz.explain: Diffuse 4f orbitals shield poorly, so effective nuclear charge rises steadily and the size shrinks.
steps: 4f orbitals are diffuse and shield one another imperfectly.
Effective nuclear charge rises steadily, so size shrinks: lanthanoid contraction.
Answer: Imperfect shielding of one 4f electron by another
quiz.mistake: Thinks the nuclear charge decreases

quiz.q: Why is Ce⁴⁺ a strong oxidising agent in aqueous solution?
options: It tends to return to the common +3 state by gaining an electron
quiz.explain: E°(Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺) = +1.74 V, so Ce⁴⁺ is readily reduced to Ce³⁺.
steps: The common state of cerium is +3.
Ce⁴⁺ gains an electron to return to Ce³⁺ (E° = +1.74 V), so it is a strong oxidant.
Answer: It tends to return to the common +3 state by gaining an electron
quiz.mistake: Gives the reason for Eu²⁺ instead

quiz.q: Which lanthanoid ion is a strong reducing agent?
quiz.explain: Eu²⁺ (4f⁷) is readily oxidised to the common Eu³⁺ state.
steps: Eu²⁺ (4f⁷) tends to reach the common +3 state.
It loses an electron easily, so it is a strong reducing agent.
Answer: Eu²⁺
quiz.mistake: Picks an ion in a higher oxidation state

quiz.q: How does the basic strength of lanthanoid hydroxides change from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃?
quiz.explain: Smaller Ln³⁺ ions polarise OH⁻ more and hold it more covalently, so basicity falls.
steps: From La³⁺ to Lu³⁺ the ion gets smaller.
Smaller ions hold OH⁻ more covalently, so basicity decreases.
Answer: It decreases
quiz.mistake: Assumes basic strength increases with atomic number

quiz.q: What is misch metal mainly composed of?
options: About 95% lanthanoid metal and 5% iron, with traces of S, C, Ca and Al
quiz.explain: Misch metal is a lanthanoid-rich alloy used in magnesium alloys for bullets, shells and lighter flints.
steps: Misch metal is a lanthanoid-rich alloy.
It is about 95% lanthanoid metal and 5% iron, with traces of S, C, Ca and Al.
Answer: About 95% lanthanoid metal and 5% iron, with traces of S, C, Ca and Al
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with steel or brass

quiz.q: What is formed when a lanthanoid reacts with water?
quiz.explain: Lanthanoids are reactive metals; they form hydroxides and release hydrogen.
steps: Lanthanoids are reactive metals.
With water they form Ln(OH)₃ and release H₂.
Answer: Ln(OH)₃ and H₂
quiz.mistake: Thinks lanthanoids are unreactive like noble metals

quiz.q: Assertion (A): It is difficult to separate lanthanoids from one another. Reason (R): Due to lanthanoid contraction, their ionic radii and chemical properties are very similar.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Similar size and charge make their chemistry nearly identical, so separation is hard.
steps: A: lanthanoids are hard to separate. True.
R: lanthanoid contraction makes their radii and chemistry very similar. True.
Similar properties make separation hard, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect similar size with similar chemistry

quiz.q: What is the general electronic configuration of the lanthanoids?
quiz.explain: Lanthanoids fill the 4f subshell, with 6s² and 0 or 1 electron in 5d. 5f¹⁻¹⁴ 6d⁰⁻¹ 7s² is the actinoid pattern.
steps: Lanthanoids fill the 4f subshell after 6s².
General configuration: 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s² (5f…7s² is for actinoids).
Answer: 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s²
quiz.mistake: Confuses the 4f lanthanoids with the 5f actinoids or with the d-block

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Why do most lanthanoids show +3, yet cerium shows +4 and europium shows +2?'
teach.praise: Chirp! +3 is typical, but +4 or +2 appear when they give empty, half-filled or full 4f — and those ions are oxidants or reductants!
teach.nudge: You said +3 is common. What f-configurations make +2 and +4 possible?

revise.summary: Lanthanoids (Ce to Lu) fill 4f orbitals: 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s². Lanthanoid contraction steadily decreases radii, making 4d/5d radii similar, separation hard and Ln(OH)₃ less basic. +3 is characteristic; Ce⁴⁺ is oxidising and Eu²⁺, Yb²⁺ reducing. Misch metal is a key use.
focus: Cause and consequences of lanthanoid contraction
traps: Don't say basicity increases from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃
Don't call Eu²⁺ an oxidising agent

topics.title: The actinoids

learn.hook: Uranium fuels the reactors at Tarapur and Kudankulam, and thorium from Kerala's sands is the heart of India's three-stage nuclear programme. Both are actinoids.
points: Actinoids are the 14 elements Th (90) to Lr (103), filling 5f orbitals. General configuration 5f¹⁻¹⁴ 6d⁰⁻¹ 7s², with irregularities because 5f and 6d are close in energy (Th is 6d² 7s²).
Actinoid contraction (decrease in size across the series) is greater than lanthanoid contraction, because 5f electrons shield even more poorly than 4f electrons.

They show a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids, because 5f, 6d and 7s levels are comparable in energy. The maximum rises from +4 (Th) to +5 (Pa), +6 (U) and +7 (Np), then falls in later elements; +3 is common but not as dominant.

All actinoids are radioactive; early members have long half-lives, later ones very short. They are reactive metals, especially when finely divided; HCl attacks all of them, but HNO₃ has little effect owing to a protective oxide layer.

Compared with lanthanoids: actinoids have wider oxidation states, larger contraction, lower ionisation enthalpies (early members), more complex magnetic behaviour and are all radioactive (among lanthanoids only promethium is radioactive).

example.q: Why do actinoids show a larger number of oxidation states than lanthanoids?
steps: In actinoids, 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals have comparable energies
So varying numbers of electrons can take part in bonding
In lanthanoids, 4f is buried deeper and rarely takes part, so +3 dominates

learn.reallife: BARC's Advanced Heavy Water Reactor design is meant to use thorium, and India holds a large share of the world's thorium in its coastal monazite deposits.

games.title: Actinoid facts
items: Actinoid contraction is greater than lanthanoid contraction.
Neptunium can show the +7 oxidation state.
The maximum oxidation state reaches +7 at Np.
HNO₃ has little effect because a protective oxide layer forms.
The actinoid series runs from thorium to lawrencium.
Actinoids show fewer oxidation states than lanthanoids.

quiz.q: Why is actinoid contraction greater than lanthanoid contraction?
options: 5f electrons shield the nuclear charge more poorly than 4f electrons
quiz.explain: Poorer shielding by 5f electrons means effective nuclear charge rises more sharply across the series.
steps: 5f electrons shield nuclear charge even more poorly than 4f electrons.
So effective nuclear charge rises more sharply and the contraction is larger.
Answer: 5f electrons shield the nuclear charge more poorly than 4f electrons
quiz.mistake: Reverses the shielding comparison

quiz.q: Which element marks the beginning of the actinoid series?
quiz.explain: The 14 actinoids run from Th (90) to Lr (103).
steps: The 14 actinoids run from Th (90) to Lr (103).
So thorium begins the series.
Answer: Thorium (Z = 90)
quiz.mistake: Counts actinium as the first actinoid

quiz.q: What is the highest oxidation state shown by neptunium?
quiz.explain: The maximum oxidation state rises from +4 (Th) to +7 at Np and then falls.
steps: Maximum oxidation state rises: Th +4, Pa +5, U +6, Np +7, then falls.
Neptunium's highest is +7.
Answer: +7
quiz.mistake: Assumes actinoids are limited to +3

quiz.q: Why do actinoids show a wide range of oxidation states?
options: They have very high ionisation enthalpies
quiz.explain: Close energy levels let different numbers of electrons be used in bonding.
steps: In actinoids 5f, 6d and 7s levels are close in energy.
So different numbers of electrons can be used in bonding.
Answer: 5f, 6d and 7s energy levels are comparable
quiz.mistake: Uses the lanthanoid explanation

quiz.q: Which property is common to all actinoids?
quiz.explain: Every actinoid is radioactive; early ones have long half-lives and later ones very short.
steps: Every actinoid is radioactive.
Early ones have long half-lives; later ones very short.
Answer: They are all radioactive
quiz.mistake: Confuses actinoids with lanthanoids

quiz.q: Which lanthanoid is radioactive?
quiz.explain: Pm is the only radioactive lanthanoid; all actinoids are radioactive.
steps: All actinoids are radioactive, but among lanthanoids only one is.
That lanthanoid is promethium.
Answer: Promethium
quiz.mistake: Thinks no lanthanoid is radioactive

quiz.q: How do actinoids behave with nitric acid?
options: They dissolve violently in nitric acid
Nitric acid has little effect because a protective oxide layer forms
quiz.explain: Like some passive metals, actinoids are protected by an oxide film in HNO₃, while HCl attacks them.
steps: HCl attacks all actinoids.
Nitric acid has little effect because a protective oxide layer forms.
Answer: Nitric acid has little effect because a protective oxide layer forms
quiz.mistake: Assumes all reactive metals dissolve in HNO₃

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The chemistry of actinoids is less smooth and predictable than that of lanthanoids. Reason (R): Actinoids show a wide range of oxidation states and are radioactive.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Many oxidation states and radioactivity (making study difficult) give actinoid chemistry its complexity.
steps: A: actinoid chemistry is less smooth than lanthanoid chemistry. True.
R: actinoids show many oxidation states and are radioactive. True.
These make their chemistry complex, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link oxidation-state variety to complex chemistry

quiz.q: Thorium (Z = 90) is the first actinoid. What is its ground-state configuration?
quiz.explain: Because 5f and 6d are close in energy, thorium places its two outer electrons in 6d and has no 5f electron. Such irregularities are typical of the early actinoids (general pattern 5f¹⁻¹⁴ 6d⁰⁻¹ 7s²).
steps: 5f and 6d are close in energy in early actinoids.
Thorium places both outer electrons in 6d with no 5f electron: [Rn] 6d² 7s².
Answer: [Rn] 6d² 7s²
quiz.mistake: Fills 5f strictly by the general formula and ignores the closeness of 5f and 6d energies

teach.ask: Gappu compares two rows: 'How are actinoids different from lanthanoids?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Actinoids fill 5f, are all radioactive and show many more oxidation states. Rows apart!
teach.nudge: You mentioned one difference. What about their oxidation states and radioactivity?

revise.summary: Actinoids (Th to Lr) fill 5f orbitals with irregular configurations (Th is 6d² 7s²). Their contraction is larger than the lanthanoids' because 5f shields more poorly. They show more oxidation states (up to +7 for Np) as 5f, 6d and 7s are close in energy, and all are radioactive.
remember: Highest states: Th +4, Pa +5, U +6, Np +7
All actinoids radioactive; only Pm among lanthanoids
traps: Don't say 5f shields better than 4f
Don't start the actinoids at actinium; they start at thorium

topics.title: Applications of d- and f-block elements and reasoning on trends

learn.hook: From the steel of the Chenab rail bridge to the TiO₂ that makes paint white, transition metals build modern India. Board exams love asking 'Give reasons' about them too.
points: Iron and steels are the most important construction materials, made by alloying iron with carbon and other transition metals (Cr, Ni, Mn, V, W, Mo).
TiO₂ is used as a white pigment; MnO₂ in dry cells; Zn and Ni/Cd in batteries; Cu, Ag and Au (group 11) are coinage metals.
Catalysts: V₂O₅ (SO₂ → SO₃ in the Contact process), TiCl₄ with Al(CH₃)₃ (Ziegler catalyst) for polythene, iron in the Haber process, nickel in hydrogenation of fats.
AgBr is used in photography because it is light-sensitive.

Typical 'give reasons': high enthalpy of atomisation (unpaired d electrons, strong metallic bonds); variable oxidation states (close ns and (n−1)d energies); coloured ions (d–d transitions); catalytic power (variable oxidation states, complex formation, surface adsorption); Zr/Hf similarity (lanthanoid contraction).

example.q: Give reason: Transition metals and many of their compounds act as good catalysts.
steps: They can show variable oxidation states, forming and breaking unstable intermediates
They can form complexes with reactants
Solid metals provide a large surface for adsorption, increasing reactant concentration and weakening bonds
example.answer: Because of variable oxidation states, complex formation and surface adsorption

learn.reallife: The Chenab rail bridge in Jammu and Kashmir, the world's highest railway arch bridge, uses special steels; TiO₂ pigment made from Kerala's ilmenite sands at Kerala Minerals and Metals Ltd, Chavara, whitens paints across India.

games.title: Give-reason check
items: Zn, Cd and Hg have low melting points because they have no unpaired d electrons.
Their d¹⁰ configuration gives weak metallic bonding.
Cu²⁺ salts are blue because of d–d transitions.
Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) absorbs in the visible region and we see the complementary colour.
Zr and Hf have similar radii because of actinoid contraction.
It is due to lanthanoid contraction.
Mn shows +2 to +7 because its 3d and 4s electrons are close in energy.
So varying numbers of electrons can be used.
TiO₂ is widely used as a black pigment.
TiO₂ is a brilliant white pigment.

quiz.q: Which compound is used as a white pigment in paints?
quiz.explain: Titanium dioxide is a brilliant white, stable pigment.
steps: Titanium dioxide is a brilliant white, stable pigment.
It is used in paints.
Answer: TiO₂
quiz.mistake: Picks a coloured oxide

quiz.q: Which metals are known as coinage metals?
quiz.explain: The group 11 metals copper, silver and gold have been used for coins.
steps: Group 11 metals have been used for coins.
They are copper, silver and gold.
Answer: Cu, Ag and Au
quiz.mistake: Picks another triad of the d-block

quiz.q: What is the Ziegler catalyst used for making polythene?
quiz.explain: The titanium–aluminium catalyst system polymerises ethene.
steps: Ziegler catalyst polymerises ethene to polythene.
It is TiCl₄ with Al(CH₃)₃.
Answer: TiCl₄ with Al(CH₃)₃
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Contact process catalyst

quiz.q: Why is AgBr used in photographic films?
options: It is highly soluble in water
It is a strong oxidising agent
quiz.explain: Light decomposes AgBr locally, forming the latent image.
steps: AgBr decomposes where light falls on it.
This light sensitivity forms the image in photographic film.
Answer: It is sensitive to light
quiz.mistake: Gives an unrelated property

quiz.q: Give reason: Transition metals have high enthalpies of atomisation.
options: They have many unpaired d electrons that strengthen metallic bonding
quiz.explain: More unpaired electrons give stronger interatomic metallic bonds, which need more energy to break.
steps: Unpaired d electrons add to metallic bonding.
Stronger bonding needs more energy to atomise the metal.
Answer: They have many unpaired d electrons that strengthen metallic bonding
quiz.mistake: Credits nuclear charge alone

quiz.q: Which component of a dry cell is a compound of a transition element?
quiz.explain: Manganese dioxide is the depolariser at the cathode.
steps: The dry cell cathode mix contains MnO₂.
Mn is a transition element; NH₄Cl and graphite contain none, and Zn is not a transition element.
Answer: MnO₂
quiz.mistake: Forgets that zinc, though in the d-block, is not a transition element

quiz.q: Give reason: The 3d metals Sc and Zn form colourless compounds in their common oxidation states.
options: Sc³⁺ is 3d⁰ and Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so no d–d transitions are possible
quiz.explain: Empty or full d subshells cannot undergo d–d excitation.
steps: Sc³⁺ is 3d⁰ and Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰.
Empty or full d subshells allow no d–d transitions, so their compounds are colourless.
Answer: Sc³⁺ is 3d⁰ and Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so no d–d transitions are possible
quiz.mistake: Thinks colour depends only on the element, not its electron count

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Iron is used in the Haber process. Reason (R): Iron is the most abundant transition metal in the Earth's crust.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but iron catalyses the Haber process because of its surface and variable oxidation states, not because it is abundant.
steps: A: iron is used in the Haber process. True.
R: iron is the most abundant transition metal in the crust. True.
Abundance does not explain its catalytic action, so R is not the explanation.
Answer: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats a true fact as the explanation

teach.ask: Gappu needs help with 'Give reasons': 'Why are transition metals coloured, catalytic and magnetic all at once?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Unpaired electrons make them magnetic, d–d transitions give colour, and variable oxidation states make them catalysts!
teach.nudge: Which feature explains colour, and which one explains catalysis?

revise.summary: d- and f-block elements are vital: iron and steels for construction, TiO₂ as white pigment, MnO₂ in dry cells, Cu, Ag, Au as coinage metals, catalysts such as V₂O₅, Fe, Ni and the Ziegler catalyst, and AgBr in photography.
remember: TiO₂: white pigment; MnO₂: dry cells; AgBr: photography
V₂O₅: Contact; Fe: Haber; Ni: hydrogenation; TiCl₄ + Al(CH₃)₃: polythene
traps: Don't say iron catalyses the Haber process because it is abundant
Don't call MnO₂ the anode of a dry cell; it is the cathode depolariser

topics.title: Werner's theory and double salts

learn.hook: Haemoglobin carrying oxygen in your blood, chlorophyll capturing sunlight in a paddy leaf and the EDTA test for hard water all involve coordination compounds. Alfred Werner first made sense of them.
points: Coordination compounds are central to biology (chlorophyll, haemoglobin, vitamin B₁₂), analytical chemistry, metallurgy and industry (catalysts, electroplating, dyes).

Werner treated cobalt(III) chloride–ammonia compounds with excess AgNO₃: CoCl₃·6NH₃ (yellow) gave 3 mol AgCl, CoCl₃·5NH₃ (purple) gave 2, and CoCl₃·4NH₃ (green and violet forms) gave 1 each. He wrote them as [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃, [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂ and [CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]Cl.

Postulates: metals show primary valence (ionisable, equal to oxidation state, satisfied by negative ions) and secondary valence (non-ionisable, equal to coordination number, satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions). Secondary valence is fixed for a metal, and the groups bound by it have a definite geometry: octahedral, tetrahedral or square planar.

Double salts (e.g. carnallite KCl·MgCl₂·6H₂O, Mohr's salt FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O, potash alum KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O) dissociate completely into simple ions in water. Complex ions such as [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ in K₄[Fe(CN)₆] do not give Fe²⁺ and CN⁻ ions.

example.q: A solution of CoCl₃·5NH₃ gives 2 mol of AgCl per mole with excess AgNO₃. Write its Werner formula and state the number of ions it gives in solution.
steps: 2 Cl⁻ are ionisable (outside the bracket)
1 Cl and 5 NH₃ are bound to Co (coordination number 6)
Formula: [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂ → [CoCl(NH₃)₅]²⁺ + 2Cl⁻

learn.reallife: Mohr's salt, a double salt, is the standard reagent in CBSE practical titrations, while K₄[Fe(CN)₆] is a complex used as an anti-caking agent in some salts.

games.title: Werner compound ↔ mol AgCl per mol

quiz.q: How many moles of AgCl are precipitated when 1 mol of [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ is treated with excess AgNO₃?
quiz.explain: All three chlorides are outside the coordination sphere and are ionisable.
quiz.mistake: Thinks chlorides are bound to cobalt
steps: Ionisable Cl⁻ = 3
mol AgCl = 3
Answer: 3

quiz.q: CoCl₃·4NH₃ gives 1 mol AgCl per mol with excess AgNO₃. What is its Werner formula?
quiz.explain: Only one Cl⁻ is ionisable; the other two Cl and four NH₃ complete the coordination number of 6.
steps: 1 mol AgCl per mol means only 1 Cl⁻ is ionisable (outside the bracket).
Co(III) has coordination number 6: 2 Cl + 4 NH₃ inside the bracket.
Answer: [CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]Cl
quiz.mistake: Puts all chlorides outside the bracket

quiz.q: According to Werner, the secondary valence of a metal corresponds to its:
quiz.explain: Secondary valence (non-ionisable) equals the coordination number; primary valence equals the oxidation state.
steps: Primary valence = oxidation state (ionisable).
Secondary valence = coordination number (non-ionisable).
Answer: coordination number
quiz.mistake: Swaps primary and secondary valence

quiz.q: Which statement distinguishes a double salt from a complex?
options: Both give the same ions in water
A complex always contains water of crystallisation
A double salt contains a coordination sphere
A double salt dissociates completely into simple ions in water; a complex ion does not
quiz.explain: Mohr's salt gives Fe²⁺, NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻, but K₄[Fe(CN)₆] gives K⁺ and [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, not Fe²⁺ and CN⁻.
steps: Mohr's salt gives Fe²⁺, NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ in water: it dissociates completely.
K₄[Fe(CN)₆] gives K⁺ and intact [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, not Fe²⁺ and CN⁻.
Answer: A double salt dissociates completely into simple ions in water; a complex ion does not
quiz.mistake: Thinks complexes break into simple ions

quiz.q: How many ions does [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂ produce in aqueous solution?
quiz.explain: It gives one [CoCl(NH₃)₅]²⁺ and two Cl⁻ ions.
quiz.mistake: Counts all atoms or ligands as ions
steps: [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂ → [CoCl(NH₃)₅]²⁺ + 2Cl⁻
Total ions = 3
Answer: 3

quiz.q: Which of these is a double salt?
quiz.explain: Mohr's salt dissociates completely into Fe²⁺, NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ in water.
steps: A double salt dissociates completely into simple ions in water.
FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O (Mohr's salt) does this; the others contain complex ions.
Answer: FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O
quiz.mistake: Picks a compound with a stable complex ion

quiz.q: What shapes did Werner propose for groups bound by secondary valence?
quiz.explain: He postulated definite spatial arrangements, explaining isomerism such as the green and violet forms of CoCl₃·4NH₃.
steps: Werner said groups bound by secondary valence have definite shapes.
These are octahedral, tetrahedral or square planar.
Answer: Octahedral, tetrahedral or square planar
quiz.mistake: Thinks ligand arrangement has no definite shape

quiz.q: Assertion (A): An aqueous solution of K₄[Fe(CN)₆] does not give tests for Fe²⁺ ions. Reason (R): [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is a stable complex ion that does not dissociate into Fe²⁺ and CN⁻.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The complex ion stays intact in water, so free Fe²⁺ is not available to react.
steps: A: K₄[Fe(CN)₆] solution gives no tests for Fe²⁺. True.
R: [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is a stable complex that does not dissociate. True.
No free Fe²⁺ is released, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats the complex like a double salt

quiz.q: Which of these biologically important substances is a coordination compound of magnesium?
quiz.explain: In chlorophyll, Mg²⁺ is held by four nitrogen donor atoms of a ring ligand. Haemoglobin (Fe) and vitamin B₁₂ (Co) are other natural coordination compounds.
steps: Chlorophyll contains Mg²⁺ held by four nitrogen donor atoms of a ring.
Haemoglobin contains Fe and vitamin B₁₂ contains Co.
Answer: Chlorophyll
quiz.mistake: Does not realise that coordination compounds occur in living systems

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What did Werner discover with those cobalt–ammonia compounds and silver nitrate?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The AgCl count showed which chlorides are ionisable (primary valence) and which are bound to the metal (secondary valence)!
teach.nudge: You mentioned AgCl. What two kinds of valence did it reveal?

revise.summary: Werner explained cobalt–ammonia chlorides by primary valence (ionisable, oxidation state) and secondary valence (non-ionisable, coordination number) with definite geometry. Double salts dissociate fully into simple ions; complex ions like [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ stay intact.
remember: Double salts: carnallite, Mohr's salt, potash alum
traps: Don't count Cl inside the bracket as ionisable
Don't call K₄[Fe(CN)₆] a double salt

topics.title: Ligands, coordination number and coordination sphere

learn.hook: EDTA grabs a calcium ion like a hand with six fingers. That's why a few drops of it can tell how hard your tap water is.
points: A coordination entity is a central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ions or molecules, e.g. [CoCl₃(NH₃)₃] or [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻. The central atom acts as a Lewis acid; the ligands, which donate electron pairs, act as Lewis bases.
Ligands by number of donor atoms: unidentate (Cl⁻, H₂O, NH₃), didentate (ethane-1,2-diamine 'en', oxalate C₂O₄²⁻), polydentate (EDTA⁴⁻, hexadentate with 2 N and 4 O donors).

A di- or polydentate ligand binding through two or more atoms to the same metal forms a ring: a chelate ligand. Ambidentate ligands can bind through either of two atoms: NO₂⁻ (through N, nitrito-N, or O, nitrito-O) and SCN⁻ (through S or N).
Coordination number (CN) = number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the metal: [PtCl₆]²⁻ has CN 6, [Ni(NH₃)₄]²⁺ has CN 4, [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ and [Co(en)₃]³⁺ have CN 6.
The central atom and its ligands, written in square brackets, form the coordination sphere; ions outside it are counter ions, e.g. K⁺ in K₄[Fe(CN)₆].

example.q: Find the coordination number of the metal in [Co(en)₃]³⁺ and in [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻.
steps: en is didentate: 3 × 2 = 6 donor atoms
C₂O₄²⁻ is didentate: 3 × 2 = 6 donor atoms

learn.reallife: The EDTA titration for water hardness used by state water-testing labs works because EDTA is a hexadentate chelating ligand that holds Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ tightly.

quiz.q: What is the coordination number of Co in [Co(en)₃]³⁺?
quiz.explain: Each ethane-1,2-diamine is didentate, so 3 × 2 = 6 nitrogen atoms bind cobalt.
quiz.mistake: Counts ligands instead of donor atoms
steps: en is didentate
Answer: 6

quiz.q: What is the coordination number of Fe in K₃[Fe(C₂O₄)₃]?
quiz.explain: Each oxalate binds through two oxygen atoms: 3 × 2 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Counts the number of oxalate ions
steps: C₂O₄²⁻ is didentate
Answer: 6

quiz.q: How many donor atoms does EDTA⁴⁻ use to bind a metal ion?
quiz.explain: EDTA⁴⁻ binds through two nitrogen and four oxygen atoms, so it is hexadentate.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the four carboxylate groups
steps: 2 N + 4 O
= 6 donor atoms
Answer: 6

quiz.q: Which ligand is ambidentate?
quiz.explain: Thiocyanate can bind through S or through N.
steps: An ambidentate ligand can bind through either of two different atoms.
SCN⁻ can bind through S or N.
Answer: SCN⁻
quiz.mistake: Thinks ambidentate means 'binds through two atoms at once'

quiz.q: What is a chelate?
options: A complex with only unidentate ligands
A ring complex formed when a ligand binds the same metal through two or more donor atoms
quiz.explain: Chelating ligands like en or oxalate wrap around the metal, forming a ring.
steps: A ligand binding the same metal through two or more donor atoms forms a ring.
Such a ring complex is a chelate.
Answer: A ring complex formed when a ligand binds the same metal through two or more donor atoms
quiz.mistake: Confuses chelating with ambidentate

quiz.q: In K₄[Fe(CN)₆], what are the counter ions?
quiz.explain: Ions outside the square bracket that balance its charge are counter ions.
steps: Ions outside the square bracket balance its charge.
In K₄[Fe(CN)₆] these are the K⁺ ions.
Answer: K⁺ ions
quiz.mistake: Thinks ligands are counter ions

quiz.q: In a coordination entity, the central metal ion acts as a:
quiz.explain: Ligands donate lone pairs to the metal, which accepts them.
steps: Ligands donate lone pairs; the metal accepts them.
An electron-pair acceptor is a Lewis acid.
Answer: Lewis acid, accepting electron pairs
quiz.mistake: Reverses the electron-pair roles

quiz.q: Assertion (A): NO₂⁻ is an ambidentate ligand. Reason (R): It can coordinate to a metal through either its nitrogen or one of its oxygen atoms.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Binding through N gives nitrito-N and through O gives nitrito-O; this is the definition of ambidentate.
steps: A: NO₂⁻ is ambidentate. True.
R: it can bind through N or through O. True.
Binding through either atom is the definition, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks NO₂⁻ binds through both atoms simultaneously

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is the difference between an ambidentate and a didentate ligand?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A didentate ligand bonds through two atoms at once; an ambidentate one can bond through either of two atoms!
teach.nudge: Which type binds through two atoms at the same time, and which one chooses between two?

revise.summary: A coordination entity has a central metal (Lewis acid) bonded to ligands (Lewis bases). Ligands are unidentate, didentate or polydentate; chelates form rings and ambidentate ligands bind through either of two atoms. Coordination number counts donor atoms.
remember: Didentate: en, C₂O₄²⁻; hexadentate: EDTA⁴⁻ (2 N + 4 O)
Ambidentate: NO₂⁻ (N or O), SCN⁻ (S or N)
CN = number of donor atoms bonded to the metal
traps: Don't count ligands instead of donor atoms for CN
Don't call the metal a Lewis base

topics.title: Coordination polyhedra, oxidation number and types of complexes

learn.hook: Board papers almost always ask: 'Find the oxidation state and coordination number of the metal.' Two quick sums and you have four marks.
points: The coordination polyhedron is the spatial arrangement of ligand atoms around the metal: octahedral ([Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺), square planar ([Ni(CN)₄]²⁻) or tetrahedral ([Ni(CO)₄]).
Oxidation number of the central atom = the charge it would carry if all ligands were removed with their electron pairs. Find it from: overall charge = x + sum of ligand charges.
Ligand charges: NH₃, H₂O, CO, en are 0; Cl⁻, CN⁻, OH⁻, NO₂⁻ are −1; C₂O₄²⁻ and SO₄²⁻ are −2; EDTA⁴⁻ is −4.
Homoleptic complexes have only one kind of ligand ([Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺); heteroleptic complexes have more than one kind ([Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺).

example.q: Find the oxidation state and coordination number of the metal in K₃[Fe(C₂O₄)₃].
steps: Complex ion charge = −3 (three K⁺ outside)
Oxalate is didentate: CN = 3 × 2 = 6

learn.reallife: The cisplatin given as chemotherapy at Indian cancer centres is a heteroleptic square-planar Pt(II) complex.

quiz.q: What is the oxidation state of Fe in K₄[Fe(CN)₆]?
quiz.explain: Complex ion is [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻: x + 6(−1) = −4, so x = +2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the charge of CN⁻
steps: Answer: 2

quiz.q: What is the oxidation state of Cu in [Cu(CN)₄]³⁻?
quiz.mistake: Assumes copper is always +2
steps: Answer: 1

quiz.q: What is the oxidation state of Co in [CoCl(NH₃)₅]Cl₂?
quiz.explain: The complex ion is [CoCl(NH₃)₅]²⁺: x + (−1) + 0 = +2, so x = +3.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the chloride inside the bracket
steps: Complex charge = +2
Answer: 3

quiz.q: What is the geometry of [Ni(CO)₄]?
quiz.explain: Ni(CO)₄ is a tetrahedral complex with Ni in the zero oxidation state.
steps: Ni(CO)₄ has Ni(0) with four CO ligands.
Its geometry is tetrahedral.
Answer: Tetrahedral
quiz.mistake: Assumes all four-coordinate complexes are square planar

quiz.q: Which complex is heteroleptic?
quiz.explain: It has two kinds of ligands, NH₃ and Cl⁻.
steps: Heteroleptic means more than one kind of ligand.
[Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺ has NH₃ and Cl⁻; the others have one kind.
Answer: [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺
quiz.mistake: Confuses the number of ligands with the number of ligand types

quiz.q: What are the oxidation state and coordination number of Pt in [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]?
quiz.explain: x + 0 + 2(−1) = 0 gives +2; four donor atoms are bonded, so CN = 4.
steps: Oxidation state: x + 2(0) + 2(−1) = 0, so x = +2.
Four donor atoms (2 N + 2 Cl), so CN = 4.
Answer: +2 and 4
quiz.mistake: Counts NH₃ as charged

quiz.q: What is the oxidation state of Cr in [Cr(en)₃]Cl₃?
quiz.explain: en is neutral, so x = +3 to balance three Cl⁻ counter ions.
quiz.mistake: Counts en as charged ligands
steps: [Cr(en)₃]³⁺
Answer: 3

quiz.q: Assertion (A): [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is a homoleptic complex. Reason (R): The metal is bound to only one kind of donor group.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Only NH₃ ligands are present, which is the meaning of homoleptic.
steps: A: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is homoleptic. True.
R: the metal is bound to only one kind of donor group. True.
That is the meaning of homoleptic, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Confuses homoleptic with heteroleptic

teach.ask: Gappu has a board question: 'How do I quickly find the oxidation state of the metal in a complex?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Add up the ligand charges, set the total equal to the complex's charge and solve for the metal. Four marks done!
teach.nudge: What do you need to know about the ligands, and what must they add up to with the metal?

revise.summary: The coordination polyhedron is the arrangement of ligand atoms: octahedral, square planar or tetrahedral. The metal's oxidation number = overall charge − sum of ligand charges. Homoleptic complexes have one kind of ligand; heteroleptic have more than one.
remember: Neutral: NH₃, H₂O, CO, en; −1: Cl⁻, CN⁻, OH⁻, NO₂⁻; −2: C₂O₄²⁻; −4: EDTA⁴⁻
traps: Don't forget counter ions when finding the complex ion's charge
Don't confuse oxidation number with coordination number

topics.title: IUPAC nomenclature of coordination compounds

learn.hook: 'Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II)' sounds like a tongue-twister, but it follows a handful of clear rules. Master them and naming questions become free marks.
points: Formulas: the central atom is written first, followed by ligands in alphabetical order; polydentate ligands are also listed alphabetically (abbreviations in parentheses). The whole entity is enclosed in square brackets, with the charge outside: K₃[Fe(CN)₆], [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃.
Names: cation first, then anion (for both positive and negative complexes). Within the complex, ligands are named in alphabetical order before the metal.
Anionic ligands end in -o: chlorido, cyanido, hydroxido, oxalato, nitrito-N. Neutral ligands keep their names, except aqua (H₂O), ammine (NH₃), carbonyl (CO) and nitrosyl (NO).
Prefixes di-, tri-, tetra- show the number of simple ligands; bis-, tris-, tetrakis- are used for ligands whose names already contain a numerical prefix, e.g. bis(ethane-1,2-diamine).

The oxidation state is given in Roman numerals in parentheses. If the complex is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate (cobaltate, zincate; Latin forms for Fe → ferrate, Cu → cuprate, Ag → argentate, Au → aurate). A neutral complex has no counter ion.

example.q: Name [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)Cl]Cl₂.
steps: Complex is a cation: Co is +3 (x + 0 + 0 − 1 = +2)
Ligands alphabetically: ammine, aqua, chlorido
tetraammine + aqua + chlorido + cobalt(III), then the counter anion

learn.reallife: Chemical suppliers in India label reagent bottles with IUPAC names such as potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III), so lab technicians never confuse the Fe(II) and Fe(III) salts.

games.title: Build the IUPAC name of K₃[Cr(C₂O₄)₃]
games.prompt: Arrange the parts in the order they are written
items: Count and name the ligands: trioxalato
Name the metal with -ate since the complex is an anion: chromate

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂?
quiz.explain: Ligands alphabetical (ammine before chlorido); Co is +3; the complex is a cation, so no -ate.
steps: Ligands alphabetically: ammine (×5 → pentaammine) then chlorido.
Co: x + 0 + (−1) = +2, so Co(III); a cation, so no -ate; counter ion chloride.
Answer: Pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride
quiz.mistake: Uses -ate for a cationic complex or gets the oxidation state wrong

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of K₃[Fe(CN)₆]?
quiz.explain: The complex anion takes the Latin -ate form ferrate; x + 6(−1) = −3 gives Fe(III).
steps: Complex anion [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻: x + 6(−1) = −3, so Fe(III).
Anionic complex takes the Latin -ate name: ferrate; potassium first.
Answer: Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III)
quiz.mistake: Forgets -ate for an anionic complex

quiz.q: What is the formula of tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride?
quiz.explain: Co(III) with one Cl⁻ ligand gives a +2 complex ion, which needs two Cl⁻ counter ions.
steps: Ligands: 4 NH₃, 1 H₂O, 1 Cl⁻ on Co(III).
Complex charge = +3 − 1 = +2, so two Cl⁻ counter ions: [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)Cl]Cl₂.
Answer: [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)Cl]Cl₂
quiz.mistake: Miscounts counter ions

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of [CoCl₂(en)₂]Cl?
quiz.explain: 'bis' is used because the ligand name contains 'di'; chlorido comes before ethane-1,2-diamine alphabetically; Co is +3.
steps: Co: x + 2(−1) + 0 = +1, so Co(III); cation, so no -ate.
Chlorido before ethane-1,2-diamine alphabetically; 'bis' because the ligand name contains 'di'.
Answer: Dichloridobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) chloride
quiz.mistake: Uses 'di' instead of 'bis' for a ligand name that already has a numerical prefix

quiz.q: What is the formula of potassium tetrahydroxidozincate(II)?
quiz.explain: Zn(II) with four OH⁻ gives [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻, which needs two K⁺; the cation is written first.
steps: Zn(II) with four OH⁻: charge +2 − 4 = −2, so [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻.
Two K⁺ balance it, cation written first: K₂[Zn(OH)₄].
Answer: K₂[Zn(OH)₄]
quiz.mistake: Miscounts the charge on the complex anion

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name for the ligand H₂O in a complex?
quiz.explain: Neutral ligands keep their names except aqua, ammine, carbonyl and nitrosyl.
steps: Neutral ligands keep their names except a few.
H₂O is named aqua.
Answer: Aqua
quiz.mistake: Writes 'water' or confuses it with OH⁻

quiz.q: What is the IUPAC name of [Ag(NH₃)₂][Ag(CN)₂]?
quiz.explain: The cation is named first without -ate; the anionic complex uses the Latin name argentate.
steps: Cation [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ is named first, without -ate: diamminesilver(I).
Anion [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ uses the Latin name: dicyanidoargentate(I).
Answer: Diamminesilver(I) dicyanidoargentate(I)
quiz.mistake: Uses -ate for the cationic part

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In the name of an anionic complex, the metal name ends in -ate. Reason (R): Anionic ligands in a complex end in -o.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both rules are true, but the -o ending of anionic ligands does not explain why the metal takes -ate.
steps: A: an anionic complex's metal name ends in -ate. True.
R: anionic ligands end in -o. True.
The ligand rule does not explain the metal's -ate ending, so R is not the explanation.
Answer: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats two separate naming rules as cause and effect

teach.ask: Gappu tries to name K₄[Fe(CN)₆]: 'Why is it ferrate and not iron, and why (II)?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The complex is an anion, so iron becomes ferrate, and (II) shows its oxidation state. Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II)!
teach.nudge: Is the complex a cation or an anion, and how does that change the metal's name?

revise.summary: In formulas the metal comes first, then ligands alphabetically, in square brackets. In names the cation comes first; ligands are named alphabetically before the metal, anionic ligands end in -o, the oxidation state is in Roman numerals and anionic complexes end in -ate.
remember: Fe → ferrate, Cu → cuprate, Ag → argentate, Au → aurate
traps: Don't use -ate for cationic complexes
Don't alphabetise by prefixes like di- or tetra-

topics.title: Stereoisomerism: geometrical and optical

learn.hook: Cisplatin cures certain cancers; its trans isomer does not. Same atoms, same bonds, different arrangement in space — that's stereoisomerism.
points: Isomers have the same formula but different arrangements. Stereoisomers differ in spatial arrangement (geometrical, optical); structural isomers differ in bonds (linkage, coordination, ionisation, solvate).

Geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism: square planar [MX₂L₂], e.g. [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], shows cis and trans forms; octahedral [MX₂L₄], e.g. [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺, also shows cis and trans. Tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism.
Octahedral [MA₃B₃], e.g. [Co(NH₃)₃(NO₂)₃], shows fac (three identical ligands on one face) and mer (on a meridian) isomers.

Optical isomers (enantiomers, d and l forms) are non-superimposable mirror images. Common in octahedral complexes with didentate ligands: [Co(en)₃]³⁺ and cis-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ are optically active; trans-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ is not (it has a plane of symmetry).
So [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ has 3 stereoisomers: trans (optically inactive) and a pair of cis enantiomers.

example.q: How many stereoisomers does [PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ have?
steps: Geometrical: cis and trans
trans has a plane of symmetry: optically inactive
cis is chiral: exists as d and l forms
Total = 1 (trans) + 2 (cis d, l)

learn.reallife: Cancer specialists at AIIMS and Tata Memorial use cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]; the trans isomer is far less effective as a drug.

games.title: Optical activity
items: It has a plane of symmetry, so it is optically inactive.
cis-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ exists as d and l forms.
Tetrahedral MA₂B₂ complexes show geometrical isomerism.
All tetrahedral positions are adjacent, so no cis–trans forms exist.
Enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.
d rotates it to the right and l to the left.

quiz.q: How many geometrical isomers does square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] have?
quiz.explain: The two Cl can be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans).
quiz.mistake: Thinks four-coordinate complexes have no isomers
steps: cis and trans
Total = 2
Answer: 2

quiz.q: How many stereoisomers does [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ have?
quiz.explain: trans (one, optically inactive) + cis (d and l) = 3.
quiz.mistake: Counts only cis and trans, missing optical isomers
steps: trans: 1
cis: d + l = 2
Total = 3
Answer: 3

quiz.q: Which complex shows fac–mer isomerism?
quiz.explain: Octahedral MA₃B₃ complexes show fac and mer forms.
steps: fac–mer isomerism occurs in octahedral MA₃B₃ complexes.
[Co(NH₃)₃(NO₂)₃] is MA₃B₃.
Answer: [Co(NH₃)₃(NO₂)₃]
quiz.mistake: Confuses fac–mer with cis–trans isomerism

quiz.q: Why do tetrahedral complexes not show geometrical isomerism?
options: All four positions in a tetrahedron are adjacent to one another
quiz.explain: Any two positions are equivalent and adjacent, so no cis–trans distinction exists.
steps: In a tetrahedron every position is adjacent to every other.
So there is no cis or trans distinction.
Answer: All four positions in a tetrahedron are adjacent to one another
quiz.mistake: Thinks tetrahedral geometry is like square planar

quiz.q: Which complex is optically active?
quiz.explain: With three didentate en ligands, the complex and its mirror image are non-superimposable.
steps: Three didentate en ligands make [Co(en)₃]³⁺ chiral.
Its mirror image is non-superimposable, so it is optically active; trans forms and [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ are not.
Answer: [Co(en)₃]³⁺
quiz.mistake: Picks a complex with a plane of symmetry

quiz.q: What are optical isomers of a complex called?
quiz.explain: Non-superimposable mirror images are enantiomers (d and l forms).
steps: Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images.
They are called enantiomers (d and l).
Answer: Enantiomers
quiz.mistake: Confuses optical isomers with structural isomers

quiz.q: Which type of isomerism does [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺ show?
quiz.explain: Two Cl can be cis or trans; neither form is chiral, so there is no optical isomerism.
steps: [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺ is octahedral MX₂L₄: the two Cl can be cis or trans.
Neither form is chiral, so only geometrical isomerism.
Answer: Geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism only
quiz.mistake: Assumes every cis isomer is optically active

quiz.q: Assertion (A): trans-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ is optically inactive. Reason (R): It has a plane of symmetry.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: A molecule with a plane of symmetry is superimposable on its mirror image, so it cannot be optically active.
steps: A: trans-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ is optically inactive. True.
R: it has a plane of symmetry. True.
A plane of symmetry makes it superimposable on its mirror image, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks all complexes with en are chiral

teach.ask: Gappu looks in a mirror: 'How do I know if a complex shows optical isomerism?'
teach.praise: Chirp! If its mirror image can't be superimposed (no plane of symmetry), it has d and l forms!
teach.nudge: What test do you apply to the mirror image, and what feature rules optical activity out?

revise.summary: Stereoisomers differ in spatial arrangement. Square planar MX₂L₂ and octahedral MX₂L₄ show cis–trans isomerism; octahedral MA₃B₃ shows fac–mer; tetrahedral complexes show none. Chiral octahedral complexes with didentate ligands, like [Co(en)₃]³⁺ and cis-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺, are optically active.
focus: Geometrical isomerism in square planar and octahedral complexes
traps: Don't give tetrahedral complexes cis–trans isomers
Don't call trans-[PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ optically active

topics.title: Structural isomerism: linkage, coordination, ionisation and solvate

learn.hook: [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂ comes in a red form and a yellow form. The only difference is which atom of NO₂⁻ holds on to cobalt.
points: Linkage isomerism arises with ambidentate ligands: [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂ is red when NO₂⁻ binds through O (nitrito-O) and yellow when it binds through N (nitrito-N).
Coordination isomerism arises from interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic complexes: [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] and [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆].
Ionisation isomerism: a counter ion and a ligand swap places, so different ions are produced in solution: [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br and [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄.
Solvate (hydrate) isomerism: water is a ligand in one isomer and water of crystallisation in another: [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet), [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O (grey-green), [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl·2H₂O (dark green).

example.q: How can you tell [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br from [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ in the lab?
steps: [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br gives free Br⁻: AgNO₃ gives a pale yellow AgBr precipitate
[Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ gives free SO₄²⁻: BaCl₂ gives a white BaSO₄ precipitate
They are ionisation isomers
example.answer: Test with AgNO₃ (for Br⁻) and BaCl₂ (for SO₄²⁻)

learn.reallife: Pigment chemists working on paints and inks look for compounds with the right colour, and linkage isomers show how one atom's switch can change a compound from red to yellow.

items.text: Ambidentate ligands give ___ isomerism.
Swapping a ligand with a counter ion gives ___ isomerism.
Exchanging ligands between a cationic and an anionic complex gives ___ isomerism.
Water inside versus outside the coordination sphere gives ___ isomerism.

quiz.q: [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂ exists as red and yellow forms. What type of isomerism is this?
quiz.explain: NO₂⁻ binds through O in one form and through N in the other.
steps: NO₂⁻ binds through O in one form (red) and through N in the other (yellow).
Different donor atoms of an ambidentate ligand give linkage isomerism.
Answer: Linkage isomerism
quiz.mistake: Confuses ligand-atom switching with counter-ion swapping

quiz.q: [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] and [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆] are examples of:
quiz.explain: The ligands NH₃ and CN⁻ are interchanged between the cationic and anionic complexes.
steps: NH₃ and CN⁻ swap between the cationic and anionic complexes.
Interchange of ligands between two complex ions is coordination isomerism.
Answer: coordination isomers
quiz.mistake: Calls any ligand rearrangement linkage isomerism

quiz.q: Which pair shows ionisation isomerism?
quiz.explain: A ligand and a counter ion exchange places, giving different ions in solution.
steps: In ionisation isomers a ligand and a counter ion exchange places.
[Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br and [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ give different ions in solution.
Answer: [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br and [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄
quiz.mistake: Confuses ionisation with solvate isomerism

quiz.q: [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet) and [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl·2H₂O (dark green) are:
quiz.explain: Water moves between the coordination sphere and the crystal lattice.
steps: Water is a ligand in one and water of crystallisation in the other.
That is solvate (hydrate) isomerism.
Answer: solvate (hydrate) isomers
quiz.mistake: Treats them as ionisation isomers only

quiz.q: In the yellow isomer of [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂, through which atom is the NO₂⁻ ligand bound?
options: Both N and O at once
quiz.explain: The yellow form is the nitrito-N isomer; the red form is nitrito-O.
steps: The red form is nitrito-O.
The yellow form is nitrito-N: bound through nitrogen.
Answer: Nitrogen
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the colours of the two forms

quiz.q: How many moles of AgCl are precipitated by 1 mol of [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O with excess AgNO₃?
quiz.explain: Only the two Cl⁻ outside the bracket are ionisable.
quiz.mistake: Counts the coordinated chloride too
steps: Ionisable Cl⁻ = 2
mol AgCl = 2
Answer: 2

quiz.q: Which test distinguishes [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ from [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br?
options: BaCl₂ gives a white precipitate only with [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄
BaCl₂ gives a precipitate only with [Co(NH₃)₅(SO₄)]Br
AgNO₃ gives a precipitate with both
Both give no reaction with any reagent
quiz.explain: Only the isomer with SO₄²⁻ outside the bracket releases free sulphate to form BaSO₄.
steps: BaCl₂ tests for free SO₄²⁻.
Only [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ has sulphate outside the bracket, giving white BaSO₄.
Answer: BaCl₂ gives a white precipitate only with [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄
quiz.mistake: Thinks coordinated ions are free in solution

quiz.q: Assertion (A): [Co(NH₃)₅(SCN)]²⁺ can show linkage isomerism. Reason (R): SCN⁻ is an ambidentate ligand.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: SCN⁻ can bind through S or N, giving two linkage isomers.
steps: A: [Co(NH₃)₅(SCN)]²⁺ can show linkage isomerism. True.
R: SCN⁻ is ambidentate. True.
Binding through S or N gives linkage isomers, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

teach.ask: Gappu mixes up isomers: 'How is linkage isomerism different from ionisation isomerism?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Linkage isomers switch the donor atom of an ambidentate ligand; ionisation isomers swap a ligand with a counter ion!
teach.nudge: Which kind involves an ambidentate ligand, and which kind changes the ions released in solution?

revise.summary: Structural isomers differ in bonding: linkage (ambidentate NO₂⁻ or SCN⁻ binding via different atoms), coordination (ligands swapped between cation and anion complexes), ionisation (ligand and counter ion swap) and solvate or hydrate (water as ligand vs water of crystallisation).
focus: Four types of structural isomerism with examples
traps: Don't confuse linkage with ionisation isomerism
Don't expect BaCl₂ to precipitate sulphate held inside the bracket

topics.title: Valence bond theory and magnetic properties

learn.hook: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is diamagnetic while [CoF₆]³⁻ is strongly paramagnetic, though both contain Co³⁺. Valence bond theory explains this with hybrid orbitals.
points: In VBT the metal uses hybrid orbitals to accept ligand electron pairs: CN 4 → sp³ (tetrahedral) or dsp² (square planar); CN 6 → d²sp³ (inner orbital) or sp³d² (outer orbital), both octahedral.

[Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺: Co³⁺ (3d⁶); NH₃ causes pairing, freeing two 3d orbitals → d²sp³, inner orbital, low spin, diamagnetic. [CoF₆]³⁻: no pairing; uses 4d → sp³d², outer orbital, high spin, 4 unpaired electrons, paramagnetic.
[Ni(CN)₄]²⁻: Ni²⁺ (3d⁸); CN⁻ pairs the two unpaired electrons → dsp², square planar, diamagnetic. [NiCl₄]²⁻: no pairing → sp³, tetrahedral, 2 unpaired, paramagnetic.

The measured magnetic moment tells the number of unpaired electrons (μ = √[n(n + 2)] BM) and hence the hybridisation and geometry, e.g. [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ (1 unpaired, d²sp³) vs [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (5 unpaired, sp³d²).

Limitations of VBT: it does not explain colour, gives no quantitative interpretation of magnetic data or thermodynamic/kinetic stability, does not distinguish weak and strong ligands, and cannot exactly predict whether a 4-coordinate complex is tetrahedral or square planar.

example.q: Predict the hybridisation, shape and magnetic behaviour of [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻.
steps: Ni²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁸, 2 unpaired electrons
Strong-field CN⁻ forces pairing, leaving one 3d orbital empty
One 3d + 4s + two 4p → dsp²

learn.reallife: Research labs in India, such as those at IISc Bengaluru, measure the magnetic moments of newly made complexes to work out how their d electrons are arranged.

steps: d²sp³ uses the inner (n−1)d orbitals, i.e. 3d.

A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

teach.ask: Gappu stares at two cobalt complexes: 'Why is [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ diamagnetic but [CoF₆]³⁻ paramagnetic?'
teach.praise: Chirp! NH₃ pairs the electrons (d²sp³, inner orbital, diamagnetic); F⁻ doesn't (sp³d², outer orbital, 4 unpaired)!
teach.nudge: What does NH₃ do to the d electrons that F⁻ does not, and which hybridisation results?

revise.summary: In valence bond theory the metal hybridises orbitals to accept ligand pairs: sp³ (tetrahedral), dsp² (square planar), d²sp³ (inner orbital) or sp³d² (outer orbital octahedral). Strong ligands pair electrons; magnetic moment reveals hybridisation. VBT cannot explain colour.
focus: Hybridisation and geometry for CN 4 and 6
remember: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻: dsp², square planar, diamagnetic; [NiCl₄]²⁻: sp³, tetrahedral, paramagnetic
traps: Don't call [NiCl₄]²⁻ square planar

topics.title: Crystal field theory: splitting, spectrochemical series and spin

learn.hook: Crystal field theory treats ligands as point charges that push d orbitals apart in energy. That simple idea explains colour and magnetism together.
points: In an octahedral field, the five degenerate d orbitals split: t₂g (dxy, dyz, dxz) are lowered by 0.4Δo and eg (dx²−y², dz²) are raised by 0.6Δo. Δo is the crystal field splitting energy.
Spectrochemical series (increasing Δo): I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < edta⁴⁻ < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO.
For d⁴–d⁷ ions, the fourth electron can pair in t₂g or enter eg. If Δo < P (pairing energy, weak field) → high spin, e.g. d⁴ as t₂g³eg¹. If Δo > P (strong field) → low spin, e.g. d⁴ as t₂g⁴eg⁰.

In a tetrahedral field the splitting is reversed (e lower, t₂ higher) and smaller: Δt = (4/9)Δo. Because Δt is small, pairing is rarely favoured and low-spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely observed.

example.q: Write the d-electron configuration of a d⁶ ion in an octahedral field with (i) Δo < P and (ii) Δo > P, and count the unpaired electrons.
steps: Weak field (Δo < P): t₂g⁴eg², four unpaired electrons
Strong field (Δo > P): t₂g⁶eg⁰, no unpaired electrons
example.answer: High spin t₂g⁴eg² (4 unpaired); low spin t₂g⁶ (0 unpaired)

learn.reallife: The deep blue of the copper(II) ammonia complex that students see in Class 12 salt analysis comes from a crystal-field splitting that absorbs orange-red light.

revise.summary: In an octahedral field d orbitals split into lower t₂g (−0.4Δo) and higher eg (+0.6Δo). The spectrochemical series ranks ligands by Δo. For d⁴–d⁷, Δo < P gives high spin and Δo > P low spin. Tetrahedral splitting is reversed and smaller: Δt = (4/9)Δo.
remember: t₂g: dxy, dyz, dxz (−0.4Δo); eg: dx²−y², dz² (+0.6Δo)
I⁻ < Br⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO
traps: Don't put dxy in the eg set
Don't say anionic ligands are always strong field

topics.title: Colour in coordination compounds and limits of CFT

learn.hook: Ruby and emerald both owe their colour to Cr³⁺ ions, yet one is red and the other green. The surrounding crystal field makes the difference.
points: A complex absorbs light whose energy matches a d–d transition (from t₂g to eg in octahedral complexes); we see the complementary colour of the absorbed light.

[Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (d¹) absorbs in the blue-green region and appears violet. Without ligands there is no splitting and no colour: anhydrous CuSO₄ is white but CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue; heating [Ti(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ to remove water makes it colourless.
Changing the ligand changes Δo and the colour: green [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ turns violet as en replaces water, forming [Ni(en)₃]²⁺.
Gemstones: ruby is Al₂O₃ with about 0.5–1% Cr³⁺; emerald has Cr³⁺ in beryl (Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈). The different surroundings give different splitting and colours.

Limitations of CFT: ligands are treated as point charges, so anionic ligands should give the greatest splitting, but they lie at the weak end of the spectrochemical series; CFT also ignores the covalent character of metal–ligand bonding.

example.q: Explain why [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is violet, and why the compound becomes colourless when heated to remove the water ligands.
steps: Ti³⁺ is 3d¹; in [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ the electron sits in t₂g
It absorbs blue-green light to jump to eg
The transmitted complementary colour is violet; without ligands there is no splitting and no d–d absorption
example.answer: Violet colour comes from a t₂g → eg transition caused by the water ligand field

learn.reallife: Jaipur's gem-cutters prize rubies and emeralds; physicists explain both colours with crystal field splitting of Cr³⁺ in different host crystals.

topics.title: Bonding in metal carbonyls

learn.hook: Nickel tetracarbonyl is so volatile that impure nickel can be purified by turning it into a gas and back. The trick lies in a special two-way bond.
points: Homoleptic carbonyls contain only CO ligands: Ni(CO)₄ is tetrahedral, Fe(CO)₅ is trigonal bipyramidal, Cr(CO)₆ is octahedral.
Mn₂(CO)₁₀ has two square pyramidal Mn(CO)₅ units joined by a Mn–Mn bond. Co₂(CO)₈ has a Co–Co bond bridged by two CO groups.

The metal–carbon bond has both σ and π character: the C atom of CO donates a lone pair into a vacant metal orbital (σ bond), and a filled metal d orbital donates electron density back into the vacant antibonding π* orbital of CO (π back-bond).
This synergic bonding strengthens the M–C bond and weakens the C≡O bond, which is why metals in very low oxidation states (such as 0) are stabilised by CO.

example.q: Explain why the metal–carbon bond in Ni(CO)₄ is strong.
steps: σ donation: lone pair on C of CO → vacant orbital of Ni
π back-donation: filled Ni d orbital → empty π* of CO
Each interaction strengthens the other (synergic effect)
example.answer: Because of synergic σ donation and π back-bonding
